Friend the Member for Whitehaven and Workington (Josh MacAlister)—to Blundell Park in Cleethorpes to meet some of our remarkable and dedicated local kinship carers and impressive council staff from the children’s services team. I am proud to have secured north-east Lincolnshire as one of the seven areas selected for the Government’s new kinship zones programme. We have already seen more than 450 children in north-east Lincolnshire benefit from a pilot of wraparound, integrated social services support and a financial package on a par with foster carers. The conversations I had that day remind us how much more there is to do. Kinship care arrangements often happen with little or no warning. Families can be given as little as an hour to decide whether they can take in a child—or several children—with whom they may not have the closest of relationships. They may have children of their own or other family responsibilities in the home. There is enormous emotional pressure and often a sense of guilt when the alternative may be sending a child formally to enter the care system.
Alistair Strathern (Hitchin) (Lab)

I thank my hon. Friend for being such a powerful champion for kinship carers across the country. Those crucial early moments are vital for any parent but, unlike with traditional parental leave, kinship carers often have to understand the caring responsibilities they are taking on at incredibly short notice, and likely against a much more traumatic backdrop than most parents have to wrestle with. It cannot be right that they do not have any access to paid leave, so they can be there for the child’s formative moments. Does my hon. Friend agree that the Government’s parental leave review is a powerful opportunity to put that injustice right?
Melanie Onn

My hon. Friend is right that this is a real opportunity—a pivotal moment, really—for the Government to put right a long-standing inequity in provision for different family arrangements. I look forward to the Minister setting out in more detail how far the Government have got with looking at that review, and when we can hope to see an outcome. Once a decision is made by the carer, children can arrive with little more than the clothes they are wearing. Carers may have no knowledge of their medical or dietary needs. Suddenly, they find themselves navigating school arrangements. It could be a grandmother navigating school arrangements, when the difference in systems is vast, and coping with new appointments and the needs of a traumatised child, often with little practical support.
Mark Sewards (Leeds South West and Morley) (Lab)

My hon. Friend is making a powerful argument and is a powerful advocate for kinship carers and the children they care for. When the Education Committee took evidence on this issue during our special educational needs and disabilities inquiry, Kinship stated that 47% of all children in kinship care have some sort of special educational need. That underlines that we should be giving kinship carers statutory paid leave so that they can meet the child’s complex needs.
Melanie Onn

I was not aware that the Education Committee did that inquiry. It goes very well with an inquiry that the APPG on kinship care did recently on the SEND needs of children in kinship care. Across Parliament, Members who have connections with kinship care communities recognise that children often arrive with additional needs, and that families often have no experience of managing or dealing with that. If a person in work, regardless of what their job is, is suddenly expected to provide for the needs of a child—it could be a physical need, or a mental, emotional or cognitive need—they have to figure it out, and in this day and age we should not expect them to take unpaid leave to navigate their way through that. They are stepping forward to provide safety and stability—the same level of care that we expect foster carers to provide. If the state provides foster care for a child in need, we make available all the necessary support, including the right to paid leave, but kinship carers are not currently entitled to that.
Ian Lavery (Blyth and Ashington) (Lab)

My hon. Friend is a tremendous advocate for kinship carers up and down this country. On more than one occasion, she has mentioned the circumstances that ordinary people find themselves in when faced with relations, close friends or potentially their own kids going into care. It is very emotional. Lots of people who accept kinship carers, such as Linda Watson in my constituency, feel the need to ensure that their children are not taken into care. They need to give them the best possible start in life, or the best way in life, at whatever age they are. A lot of kinship carers believe that a pat on the back, a rub on the back of the neck, a pat on the head and a big thank you are not enough. They need financial support so that they can give these kids, who are already in a difficult position with their family life and all the rest of it, a good start in life. In order to do that, kinship carers need the right support; they need adequate financial support.
Melanie Onn

I thank my hon. Friend for his powerful contribution. To build on that, eight in 10 kinship carers who leave their work never return to paid employment. This is not just a short-term problem; it can lead to lifelong issues. The Government have pledged to ensure that people are in work for the long term, and they are setting an example of what work means, but providing sufficient flexibility in our employment law is the right way to go to ensure that these families can be self-sufficient while providing support and love for the child. They should be able to earn a living without being penalised. My constituent Lucy was in the same position as the constituent of the hon. Member for Twickenham (Munira Wilson): she had to take a mix of sick leave and compassionate leave, which her employer very kindly jumbled together. She said, “Why should my kids be disadvantaged because the system doesn’t recognise them and doesn’t really work for them?”
Gareth Snell (Stoke-on-Trent Central) (Lab/Co-op)

What my hon. Friend is pointing out, but has not quite said yet, is that we are also thinking about the long-term costs for society. Families that step forward stop a child going into care, which is much more expensive and much more traumatic for the young person. A phased period of going back to work before going back fully stops a carer having to call on the state for support over their lifetime. The Government ought to think about this not as a potential extra cost burden somewhere, but as an investment and a genuine preventive measure that saves money while improving outcomes. What is not to like?
Melanie Onn

I could not agree more. Independent analysis commissioned by the Family Rights Group says that paid kinship leave could return over £2 into the economy for every £1 invested, so double the support provided to these families goes back into the local economy.
Ms Julie Minns (Carlisle) (Lab)

My hon. Friend is being very generous with her time. I want to go further on the point about investment and the comparison between kinship care and foster care that she mentioned earlier. One of my constituents has been a kinship carer for three children for nine years. She is also a foster carer for her grandson. She reports that because of his legal status, it has been easier for her to access the support she needs for him than for the three children she cares for as a kinship carer. Does my hon. Friend agree that in

title: Heathrow Airport Expansion
contributions: [Relevant Documents: Oral evidence taken before the Transport Committee, on Scrutiny of the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement, 14 October, 13 October, 15 September, 9 September, 8 September and 2 September, HC 482; Written evidence to the Transport Committee, on Scrutiny of the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement, reported to the House on 13 October, 14 September and 1 September 2025, HC 482; and Correspondence from the Chief Analyst, Department for Transport, to the Transport Committee, on the Heathrow expansion economic case, reported to the House on 1 September, HC 482.]
Fleur Anderson (Putney) (Lab)

I beg to move, That this House has considered Heathrow airport expansion. It is a pleasure to serve under your chairship, Sir John, and I thank all my constituents in Putney who have written to me, attended public meetings and taken part in the recent consultation on Heathrow expansion. I am really grateful to have secured today’s debate, and for the opportunity to explain why the Mayor of London, so many London MPs and so many Londoners continue to oppose the enormous expansion of Heathrow, the third runway and all that comes with it. I am also grateful to the Prime Minister and the Minister for Aviation for engaging with the concerns that I and many others have raised. The proposal on the table would significantly and adversely affect the health and wellbeing of 3 million people living near Heathrow, and there would be a 58% increase in flights. Under the expansion proposal, the number of flights would increase by 276,000 per year— 756 per day. This debate comes at an important moment in the decision-making process. It is only weeks since the Government’s consultation on the draft Heathrow expansion national policy statement closed on 1 September, and we are only days before Heathrow launches its own consultation on its expansion plans on 27 October. However, Heathrow is consulting on expansion before the Government have completed the policy framework that would govern it. That is the wrong way round. Before taking a decision of such magnitude, we should ask a simple question: knowing what we know now, would Parliament make the same decision today as it was asked to make when the Airport Commission reported and made the proposal in 2015? I do not believe that it would. In 2015, the Airport Commission’s case rested on assumptions about jobs, growth, aviation demand, sustainable aviation fuel, carbon reduction and regional economic benefits, but many of those assumptions have now been blown apart and look considerably weaker, so I am going to whizz through eight major things that have changed since 2015. I will also talk about three important things that have not changed since then. First, I am going to focus on the major central justification for expansion: the economic case, which I believe has collapsed. The Government’s own figures tell a very different story from the one we were told a decade ago. In 2015, the Airports Commission estimated that expansion could boost GDP by £20 billion to £23 billion. Earlier this year, supporters of expansion were still citing figures of around £13 billion. However, the Department for Transport’s appraisal in the HENPS document estimates a GDP increase of just 0.03% to 0.05% by the 2050s—the equivalent of roughly £900 million to £1.5 billion over decades. The headline economic benefit used to justify Heathrow expansion has therefore fallen from £20 billion to perhaps little more than £1 billion. A project once sold as transformational would now deliver an impact that is barely measurable in the context of a £3 trillion economy. Those figures would raise serious questions for any major infrastructure project. Secondly, I will talk about jobs. In 2015, the Airports Commission argued that a third runway could support about 70,000 new jobs across the UK by 2050, yet the Government’s own analysis suggests that many jobs would be relocated, rather than created. The DFT estimates that Heathrow expansion could draw around 21,400 jobs into the Heathrow area while contributing to the loss of approximately 15,200 jobs elsewhere in the UK. Moving jobs from one region to another is obviously not the same as creating new jobs. Thirdly, the premise of spreading growth across the UK has changed. The Government cannot demonstrate that the growth generated would be genuinely additional. If jobs, passengers and investment are simply drawn from other airports and regions, Britain is not creating growth; it is just relocating it. Analysis by the New Economics Foundation suggests that Birmingham airport alone could lose around 7.5 million passengers annually by 2050, alongside approximately 9,500 jobs across the airport and its supply chains. On devolution, No.10 North is going in one direction, but Heathrow expansion—being so concentrated on London and the south-east—would take us in another direction. At a time when Ministers rightly want to spread opportunity more evenly across the country, Heathrow expansion risks doing precisely the opposite.
Dr Rupa Huq (Ealing Central and Acton) (Lab)

My hon. Friend is making a really powerful point. When he was the Mayor of Manchester, the Prime Minister warned many times that Heathrow expansion would suck the life out of regional airports. Does she agree that that is now more true than ever? The Prime Minister is also really into devolution. The Mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, is also against Heathrow expansion, so the Prime Minister should listen to our Mayor, too.
Fleur Anderson

I absolutely agree with my hon. Friend. The context of this debate has changed, which is my point; things have changed since 2015. We are looking again at devolution and growth across the country, and that changed context means that Heathrow expansion really needs to be looked at again, especially when the Mayor of London opposes it so strongly. Fourthly, business travel has changed; the world that originally produced the case for the third runway no longer exists. Much of the demand modelling that was made then assumed ever-increasing business travel, but the pandemic accelerated a shift towards remote working and video conferencing, which has become permanent. Research highlighted by the New Economics Foundation shows that over the two decades before the pandemic, UK GDP grew by around 25% while business passenger numbers through UK airports showed virtually no growth at all. Today, business travel remains at a level that is about 20% below pre-pandemic levels, so the fundamental assumption about business travel no longer applies. Fifthly, assumptions about sustainable aviation fuel have also changed. Sustainable aviation fuel was meant to be the great white charger that would come galloping over the hills, and that we would all be using it, and it would be the answer to all our climate problems. However, use of it is far less than predicted and is growing more slowly than predicted. It still accounts for far less than 1% of global aviation fuel use, and even under the Government’s own plans, around 90% of aviation fuel being used in 2030 would still be conventional fuel. In effect, Parliament is being asked to approve additional emissions now on the basis that future technology might solve the problem some time later, but that hope is really not being borne out. Sixthly, the climate challenge has become far more acute. The Climate Change Committee’s conclusion in its report last month was clear—the UK does not currently have a credible pathway to reduce aviation emissions in line with net zero while accommodating Heathrow expansion. The Committee estimates that expansion would add an additional 2.4 million tonnes of carbon dioxide every year by 2050. That is roughly the equivalent of putting around half a million additional petrol-fuelled cars on Britain’s roads, all the emissions of Denmark, and greater than all the emissions of New Zealand.
Alex Sobel (Leeds Central and Headingley) (Lab/Co-op)

When I was first elected to Parliament nine years ago, we had people coming in and saying that new technology in aviation—electric planes, hydrogen planes and SAF—would significantly reduce emissions by 2025; I think that was the date given. None of that has happened. So all these assumptions are being made about new technology, which has not arrived and will not arrive. And we will break through our carbon budget just with increased aviation, particularly if we go ahead with a third runway at Heathrow. Does my hon. Friend agree?
Fleur Anderson

I absolutely agree with my hon. Friend and I thank him for that intervention, which speaks for the views of so many people, who are saying similar things. Indeed, a long time ago they were saying, “Look at the assumptions”, but now we have even more facts about those assumptions. We know what has actually come to pass and it is not all that was promised. At a time when households, motorists and businesses are being asked to reduce emissions, and after the summer of extreme weather that we have just had, why would we seek permission to increase emissions by so much? Seventhly, our understanding of the health impact of noise has changed. Noise is not just an inconvenience; it is not something for people to get used to. We now know the impact of noise on many health conditions, including heart conditions and mental health conditions. This new knowledge about the impact of noise and what that impact will be on so many millions more people really should give the Government pause for thought. At the very least, the Government should commit to a full seven-hour night-flight ban between 11 pm and 6 am, with a pathway towards an eight-hour ban in the future. That respite would be so important for my constituents. Eighthly, our expectations on air quality have changed. London is now the world’s largest clean-air zone. Putney’s high street used to be one of the most polluted in the country, but is now just the same as other high streets. That has been through a lot of hard policy and hard work. The ultra low emission zone covers every London borough and has reduced harmful nitrogen dioxide concentrations in central London by more than 50%. There has been heavy investment around improving our air quality, but this pollution from Heathrow airport would take us in the other direction. Those are eight things that have changed since 2015, and I am sure that the Minister has listened very carefully to them all, but there are three things that have not changed. First, there is no funding plan for the surface transport to go along with the airport. I have been asking this question of Treasury Ministers ever since the proposals came out: “Will the Government fund the ground transport?” No. I have been asking Heathrow, “Will Heathrow fund the ground transport?” No, it will not. We have a massive gap here given the number of people who will travel to Heathrow airport. What will they travel on? I think that that will be a real millstone around the Government’s neck in future. The second thing that has not changed is that Heathrow is the wrong location for a hub airport of this scale, for areas such as Northern Ireland—I know that we have a Member from Northern Ireland here—Liverpool, Manchester or Scotland. If anyone looked at the UK to decide where to put a hub airport, would they really put it next to one of the most densely populated parts of the whole country, or would they put it in the middle of the country? Would they locate it at an airport that already had two runways, such as Manchester’s? The third thing that has not changed is that we do not have a national aviation strategy. Why are these decisions being made piecemeal? We have Gatwick, Luton and now Heathrow; where is the overall strategy for this? What is the decision-making behind it? Why do we not step back, look at what kind of aviation growth we want and need and where we want that to be, and then put this decision within that? When the Airports Commission recommended Heathrow’s expansion in 2015, it asked the public and Parliament to accept a trade-off: to accept the noise, the environmental impacts and the disruption, because the rewards would be worth it. We were promised transformational economic growth across the United Kingdom, but, more than a decade later, we find a very different situation. Those foundations and assumptions are very weak. The projected economic gains are smaller than promised.
Alex Sobel

One concerning point that my hon. Friend did not raise is the number of houses that will be demolished and the number of people who will be displaced. Heathrow’s own assumption is fewer than 1,000, but that is really only the direct curtilage of the runway. Even a quite casual look at a map would show that the uninhabitable zone around Heathrow could be north of 5,000 homes. Who would pay for those demolitions, and for the replacements and compensation for those homeowners? That is something, alongside ground transport, that nobody is willing to pay for. That is an exceedingly large amount of money, on top of the misery caused for all those people living there.
Fleur Anderson
I absolute

title: House of Lords Reform
contributions: Dr Simon Opher (Stroud) (Lab) [R]

I beg to move, That this House has considered House of Lords reform. It is a pleasure to bring this debate to Parliament as chair of the all-party parliamentary group on House of Lords reform. A few weeks ago, I showed a group of United States doctors around Parliament, which involved sitting in the Public Gallery of the House of Lords, looking at the King Charles throne, the Woolsack and a scattering of some quite elderly peers. One doctor said, “How do these guys get in here?”. When I answered that they were appointed by their mates, they all laughed—surely I was joking. Sadly, I was not joking. Reform of the House of Lords has been on the cards for centuries. The House was actually abolished in 1649, but was reinstated a few years later, and it has been the subject of intense debate ever since. The idea of unelected peers having inherited access to Parliament alongside crony appointees controlling the laws that Parliament produces is clearly ridiculous. It is no wonder that the crisis of confidence in our political system is at an all-time high. This Government have actually taken quite big strides—probably more than others—on the long overdue removal of hereditary peers. I also welcome proposals to impose a retirement age and a minimum participation requirement, but we cannot afford to push this constitutional necessity further down the road. I will take this opportunity to set out the case for reform of the House of Lords and how we can go about implementing it. The function of our second Chamber is to scrutinise and amend legislation passed by the elected Commons. There are many exceptional Lords who do a really good job at that, but their contribution is undermined by their complete lack of legitimacy. It is simply not right that our Parliament has more unelected lawmakers than lawmakers with a mandate from the people. During the Makerfield by-election, the Prime Minister called it “scandalous” and expressed support for an early change to the Lords. One of the things that has most surprised me is learning that the House of Lords remains a self-governing institution. In the last session, we saw a handful of unelected peers, many of whom were rejected by the voters at the last election, abuse that fact to stall the progression of legislation passed by the elected Commons. The other place is also deeply unrepresentative of our country. Over 55% of peers live in London and the south-east. I know that our Prime Minister is very concerned with that, and that he has called for a senate of nations and regions to replace the Lords, so that every corner of our country is properly represented in both of our Chambers. The public also want change. Only 16% support the current status quo; 70% have little or no confidence in the institution, and a majority want an entirely elected upper Chamber. The voters gave a very clear mandate for a Labour manifesto that included a commitment to replacing the House of Lords with an alternative second Chamber, more representative of the regions and nations. What could a second Chamber look like? That is a complex issue; we should convene a commission of citizens and experts to decide on its role and make-up. It should still absolutely be possible to retain the expertise that we have there, and that is exactly what our manifesto has committed us to.
Mike Wood (Kingswinford and South Staffordshire) (Con)

The hon. Gentleman has made a good start on setting out his case. However, does he not see the irony in calling for an appointed committee of the public and experts to look at how democratic the House of Lords is?
Dr Opher
I would say that we need experts to look at how our democracy works and to devise a better way of doing it.
Ben Lake (Ceredigion Preseli) (PC)

I congratulate the hon. Member on securing this debate. Does he agree that such a consultative process might well come about from a Bill that my noble Friend, Baroness Smith of Llanfaes, has introduced to the second Chamber? It should indeed be for the experts to provide some ideas, and for us and members of the public to consult on the best way forward for the second Chamber.
Dr Opher

I have been working with Baroness Smith on her Bill. We need to get the great minds of this country to devise a good political system, one that reflects our country and gives us our best government. I suggest that we need a commission to look into the matter. That commission could take many experts. How it is actually constituted remains something we can debate. The Government have announced a commission on electoral reform; maybe that could be extended to examine the composition of the second Chamber, because that would be a holistic approach to the system. I see some hon. Members shaking their heads. I will briefly touch on an issue that many hon. Members care about: the lack of transparency in the other place. According to research by Transparency International UK, 128 peers hold paid political advisory roles that risk breaching parliamentary rules. We must strengthen the House of Lords code of conduct to put beyond doubt that legislators who serve in the House of Lords should not be lobbyists. Since 2013, almost a quarter of all nominations from political parties have been political donors—that is the ultimate cronyism. I know many hon. Members wish to speak, so in conclusion I ask the Minister to meet with the APPG on House of Lords reform to discuss how the Government intend to fulfil their manifesto commitment to consult the public on an alternative second Chamber. Will the Minister consider expanding the remit of the commission on electoral reform to cover the role and composition of the other place? It is time—to quote someone who I do not normally agree with— to “take back control.”
Sir John Hayes (in the Chair)
I remind Members to bob if they want to be called to speak. I see that a number of Members are bobbing, so I will give priority to those who applied early to speak in the debate.
Andrew Rosindell (Romford) (Reform)

It is a pleasure to serve under you, Sir John. I have been a Member of Parliament for 25 years, probably longer than anyone else in this debate, and I believe that the House of Lords, for all its faults over the years, provides a balance to an elected Chamber. I am afraid to say that the hon. Member for Stroud (Dr Opher) misses the point of the House of Lords. We do not want another elected Chamber to rival the House of Commons. We need a house of experts—or elders, if you like, Sir John—people with knowledge, expertise and experience who have served this country over many decades in different walks of life.
Mike Martin (Tunbridge Wells) (LD)
Will the hon. Member give way?
Andrew Rosindell

In a moment. We need also those who represent continuity. Sir John, you will know better than most that continuity is the foundation of the success of this nation. To ignore what has gone on in the past and to lose all that continuous wisdom from the ages is pure vandalism. We do not want another elected set of politicians who we know will be, effectively, appointed by party headquarters—the leader’s favourites will be put on some list and put into the House of Lords, even though many of them would prefer to be in the House of Commons—as a second set of politicians. I want a House of Lords that is depoliticised in many ways, so I am not keen on the fact that Labour, the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats have put so many people into the Lords who were friends of the leader at the time, or special advisers to Ministers and suchlike. What I want to see is more people who are truly representative of the whole country but can provide knowledge, expertise and experience to make our parliamentary democracy stronger and better. It cannot be right that a political party that came third at the last general election has zero representation in the House of Lords. There are 80 Lib Dem peers, yet their party received 600,000 fewer votes than Reform UK. The Greens, I believe, have three representatives—
Dr Ellie Chowns (North Herefordshire) (Green)
Two.
Andrew Rosindell

Two? Okay. Plaid Cymru also has representatives. The Democratic Unionist party has six, but only five MPs. The thing is disproportionate. There should at least be representation of all political parties. Based on the votes at the last election, there certainly need to be a number of Reform UK Members of the House of Lords.
Mike Martin

I thank the hon. Member for giving way, because there is just so much to feast upon there in one intervention. Just to draw out an inconsistency in his speech, he likes experts and history—I like them as well—yet he says that we should have an upper Chamber that is based on the votes at the last election. Presumably, those would be appointed by the parties, so how does he intend to balance those two tensions?
Andrew Rosindell

The hon. Member will know that the way it works in the House of Lords is that it is based on party appointments. The Prime Minister will make nominations; so will the Leader of the Opposition; so will the leader of the Liberal Democrats; so will the leader of the Greens. They will nominate a sprinkling of new peers every so often, usually once a year. Well, where was the invitation for the leader of Reform UK to nominate a number of Reform UK Members of the House of Lords? The hon. Member must surely accept that that is very wrong when we consider that Reform UK was the third largest party in terms of votes at the last election.
Dr Opher
Will the hon. Member give way?
Andrew Rosindell

I will in a moment. I go back to my original argument: we are getting this wrong. We will regret the day that we become just one of two elected Chambers. We will regret that day. It will create a rivalry between two sets of elected politicians, who will both claim to be truly representative of the people who have put them there, instead of having the primacy of the elected House of Commons—ultimately, we are elected by the people of this country and we can make the final decision through the Parliament Acts. At the end of the day, we do not actually have to be obedient to the House of Lords. What I do know is that, within the House of Lords, there is an opportunity to have people with enormous knowledge and expertise, whether they are former Cabinet Ministers, former ambassadors or high commissioners, heads of industry, heads of trade unions or representatives of the different faith groups. It is good to have people like that. It is right that we still have the established Church of England represented through the bishops; although, these days, they are rather more to the left than I would like, they still represent the established Church of this country.
Dr Opher
I thought that, in Reform’s manifesto, it was going to abolish the House of Lords and replace it with a much smaller, more democratic second Chamber.
Andrew Rosindell

Well, I did not stand on that manifesto. I joined Reform UK after that manifesto. I can tell the hon. Member now that that is not our policy today. We are not going to abolish the House of Lords. We are not going to engage in constitutional vandalism. Throughout the ages, we have evolved our constitutional and parliamentary democracy in a way that has given us strength and continuity, and has allowed us to change not in some radical direction, whereby minorities and people with vested interests can finish up controlling the institutions of this country, but in a way that is evolution rather than revolution. There is no requirement to abolish the House of Lords. There should not be an elected second Chamber. New Zealand got rid of its second Chamber, so it has only one elected Chamber. I would prefer that, frankly, to a second load of politicians in the House of Lords who wish that they were MPs, but could not get there, so they were put in place by their friends in party headquarters. We do not want that. If we eventually do abolish the upper House, frankly it would be better just to have one Chamber than to have a second elected Chamber, because there would be rivalry between the two. Look at it like this: if we choose carefully, change the system and make it more meritocratic in terms of experience, knowledge and the kind of people who we really want in the House of Lords, we will be buying in expertise at low cost. Otherwise, we will be paying consultants and experts that work for companies to do an effective job of scrutinising legislation. What is the point of that when we can give someone a peerage? That could be someone with vast knowledge, perhaps someone who has been an ambassador to another country, headed up an important institution or contributed to the establishment of an amazing charity, and who has vast knowledge from that. It could be someone like Sebastian Coe, the Olympic gold medallist who went on to run the London Olympics in 2012. Those people have value, but they will not stand for election, so we would lose all of them— [ Interruption. ] Well, they would not stand for election to the Lords. As I say, we would lose good people. The great and the good would go and we would finish up, as I said earlier, with people who want to be politicians but would have to settle for being second-best. That is not good enough. We should do what we have always done in this country and allow our constitution and our parliamentary

title: International Update
contributions: “With permission, I wish to make a Statement on the United Nations General Assembly and related international events that have occurred since the House last met.

Before I do so, let me first welcome my honourable friend the new Member for Holborn and St Pancras, Sagal Abdi-Wali, to her place. What a journey, from child refugee to Parliament, and what a country—that this story of hope could happen here. I know my honourable friend will enhance this House in so many ways, and I look forward to working with her.

I took a clear message to the United Nations: after a decade of turbulence, Britain is back and can be relied upon as a consistent and stable partner in an uncertain world, always upholding the shared values set out in the UN charter, rejecting aggression wherever we see it, and always steadfast in our support for Ukraine, as I assured President Zelensky at our meeting in New York.

In the three weeks since that meeting, Russian strikes have intensified even further, with more attacks on civilians: on apartment blocks housing innocent families and on buses carrying innocent children. When I spoke to President Zelensky on Saturday, he described the step change from Russia, including daylight attacks intended to break the will of Ukraine—and ours. I can tell you that that will never happen. In recent days, we have announced new funding to help Ukraine get through its fifth winter under Russian bombardment and a new sanctions package so that over 90% of Russia’s oil-producing capacity is now covered by UK sanctions.

The quickest way to get diesel back on to world markets without rewarding the aggressor is an energy ceasefire, with both sides stopping their attacks. I raised this with President Trump in New York. It is what Ukraine wants to see, so I welcome President Trump’s announcement yesterday of a reciprocal energy ceasefire. President Zelensky has assured me that Ukraine would immediately implement it when a start date is confirmed, and I will be discussing this further with him in the coming days.

NATO is a defensive alliance. We do not seek confrontation, but our resolve to defend our allies and ourselves is absolute, and I was clear in all of my meetings, including with the NATO Secretary-General in Oxfordshire, that we will meet our NATO commitments in full.

We know that Russia is conducting a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe. In Berlin last week, Chancellor Merz and I agreed a new partnership to tackle these hybrid threats. We must be clear-eyed about attempts to destabilise our democracies. It is why, in my speech to the UN General Assembly, I confirmed our commitment to establish a new centre for information defence, as recommended by the Foreign Affairs Select Committee. More broadly, this is a moment to deepen collaboration with our partners, which is why in Berlin I indicated Britain’s openness to Germany joining the Global Combat Air Programme alongside Italy and Japan.

In my meeting with President Trump, we discussed the situation in the Middle East. I confirmed Britain’s decision to send air defence and a Voyager aircraft to Saudi Arabia to provide air-to-air refuelling support. I can confirm today that it has already completed 14 operational missions. This support is needed to protect civilians. I condemn the appalling attacks on the King Khalid International Airport. We will continue to stand with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis.

Since UNGA, we have been in close contact with the US about protective security at our shared bases. I thank our police and military personnel for their swift response to the incidents at RAF Fairford and RAF Molesworth. My right honourable friend the Home Secretary will update the House on the incident at RAF Fairford, but I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been co-ordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm.

In my meeting with the President, I also raised the Falkland Islands and the clear and declared will of the islanders to remain British. I emphasised that point in my speech to the UN General Assembly and that we will also always do whatever it takes to uphold their will.

In New York, I also had a positive meeting with the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, about the forthcoming UK-EU summit. I can confirm to the House today that it will take place in Brussels on 20 November. This summit presents an opportunity to make progress on two crucial issues: boosting UK growth and controlling illegal immigration. On the table is a trade deal on food and drink products, a deal on emissions trading, progress towards linking our energy systems, a new youth experience scheme, and deeper co-operation on immigration.

The summit will also be an opportunity to raise our concerns about ‘Made in Europe’, and it is clear to me that there is an opportunity to make progress in all these areas. Together, these deals will add the equivalent of over £10 billion per year to the UK economy by 2040, with the potential to add significantly more. We should not turn our backs on this opportunity, and I hope Members from all sides of this House will get behind the Government’s efforts to land a positive outcome. It is a chance to cut costs and bureaucracy for sectors such as farming.

At present, entire truckloads of plants or fresh produce can be destroyed because of a single missing stamp or a minor paperwork delay. Fresh meat and fish spoil while waiting in trucks, and tonnes of exports have to be written off. Our largest food export, Scottish salmon, faces a 100% rate of document checks at the border, costing us around £100 million in lost exports. British burgers and other fresh meat products cannot be sold in the EU. Seed potatoes from Scotland and shellfish from Wales are banned. This is having a real impact on businesses, and the agreement on the table could reverse some of that damage. For farmers and food producers, it would lift a burden that can reach £1,400 on a single shipment. For our small businesses, it would mean no more export health certificates, which can cost up to £200 each time. For households, it would ease the pressure on prices in the supermarket. It could help lower energy costs for households and businesses alike.

In Northern Ireland, the proposed energy deal could cut wholesale energy costs by 20%. On immigration, we could link up our law enforcement efforts once again, sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals, as well as ensuring faster electronic evidence from the phones of those behind the gangs. It is in Britain’s interests to secure a deal along these lines, and I will work hard over the next five weeks to achieve that. I believe that our chances of doing so will be enhanced by being open to a discussion about our relationship with the EU in the longer term. If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, and upholding our values and security, it is a conversation that we must have. Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain. Worse, it would be a major dereliction of duty to turn away. We need to take a calm, clear-eyed, rational look at the world as it is today, to consider what is best for our country.

Our immediate priority is securing a successful outcome at the summit, and I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term. At every stage, the British public will be the boss, and I am clear that public opinion currently supports a pragmatic approach, like the one I am suggesting, but if we go into this further phase, we will proceed with care and complete transparency. This is the leadership we need to draw a line under a decade of drift and division, and to take the country forward.

Beyond Europe, a confident Britain is ready to play our part on the global stage as we take up the presidency of the G20 in 2027. I confirmed in New York that we will place artificial intelligence centre stage in our presidency, to capture the incredible opportunities it presents while guarding against the risks. Leading voices such as the president of Microsoft are saying that Britain is the world leader on AI safety, so we are well placed to take on this role, and to work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards on AI, in our G20 presidency year.

The message to the world is clear: Britain is back. On so many fronts, we are playing our part and looking confidently to the future. We are leading again, so our country can hope again. I commend this Statement to the House”.
Earl Howe (Con)

My Lords, I am grateful to the Leader of the House for allowing time for questions on this Statement. In the other place, my right honourable friend the leader of the Opposition set out some of the serious challenges that we are facing as a country, many of which cannot be solved through international engagement without serious hard work at home. As the Official Opposition, we are willing to work with the Government on defence, welfare spending, and support for our allies across the world, particularly Ukraine. The Prime Minister’s Statement was upbeat in its tone, but it was perhaps a pity that he could not have said more about the specific challenges that we are facing as a country. The Prime Minister spoke at some length about the opportunities of a new trade deal with the European Union that might cut through barriers faced by UK exporters. It was encouraging to hear him express confidence that such a deal was attainable. Can the Minister say what has led the Prime Minister to express that degree of confidence that a better deal with the EU is within reach? He said that there is a deal “on the table”, but what we did not hear was what the EU could expect us to concede in return. Will there be any red lines in our position, and if so, what will they be? On this side of the House we of course want to see stronger economic growth, but if we look at what is happening in the EU on growth, it is not encouraging. This week, Chancellor Merz of Germany, the Italian Prime Minister, Meloni, and the Belgian Prime Minister, De Wever, all called for an emergency brake mechanism to help boost the EU’s flagging economic competitiveness. That shows that EU leaders themselves recognise the economic risks of overregulation. Can the Minister explain why the Prime Minister feels that new agreements with the EU would unlock growth when EU leaders themselves are battling against overregulation within the bloc? On a specific point included in the prospective trade deal, the Prime Minister referred to energy prices in Northern Ireland. He said: “In Northern Ireland, the proposed energy deal could cut wholesale energy costs by 20%”. I emphasise the word “wholesale”. I was puzzled by that and would be glad if the Minister could explain what precisely he meant. I was heartened to see the Prime Minister’s unequivocal and steadfast support for Ukraine. That is a position on which we have had cross-party consensus since Putin’s illegal invasion, and I welcome President Zelensky’s visit today. On a specific point relating to sanctions, the Energy Minister, the noble Baroness, Lady Curran, said yesterday in the House that the United Kingdom’s ban on Russian oil “applies to all oil and oil products that originate in Russia, irrespective of the way that they enter the UK ”.—[ Official Report , 13/10/26; col. 115.] Was that statement strictly accurate? Can the Minister confirm that, under the general trade licence for sanctioned processed oil products, some Russian-derived oil products are in fact being imported into this country? Can she say when Ministers intend to discontinue that licence? The Prime Minister made a point of committing the UK to meeting our NATO commitments in full. Yesterday, the Defence Secretary warned of the risk that our allies, if attacked, would prioritise the supply of defence equipment for their own defence over agreed supplies to the United Kingdom. He went on to emphasise the strategic importance of building our sovereign defence supply capabilities. However, we understand from the Prime Minister that we will have to wait until the spending review—possibly as late as next autumn—for confirmation of when the United Kingdom will hit the interim 3% spending target. If we want to build our sovereign defence capabilities, that is a long delay that leaves our own defence manufacturing sector in limbo. Does the Minister agree with the Defence Secretary on the importance of homegrown defence? If she does agree, can she confirm that we will have to wait until next autumn before we know the date by which the Government plan to hit the 3% interim

title: Prisoner Early Release Scheme
contributions: “This Government inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse. In July 2024, men’s prisons were operating at 99% capacity. At one point, fewer than 100 places were available across the male estate. Without intervention, we risked running out of prison places, leaving courts unable to sentence offenders and police unable to make arrests.

This Government have acted to increase capacity and to reform sentencing. We have committed to delivering 14,000 prison places by 2031 and have already delivered 3,200. The last Government added just 500 net places in their time in office. We have also accelerated the removal of foreign national offenders, returning around 11,700 to their countries of origin. It is in that context that we launched the independent sentencing review in October 2024 and subsequently passed the Sentencing Act 2026 earlier this year to place the prison system on a more sustainable footing and ensure that space is always available for the most dangerous offenders. The Act also aimed to avoid the chaotic emergency release schemes carried out with little scrutiny or warning by the Conservatives.

However, we know that aspects of these changes have caused concern, and we are determined to do the right thing for victims. That is why the Government listened to the concerns raised, paused the implementation of the progression model and conducted an urgent review. As the Lord Chancellor confirmed in this House on 1 September, in addition to the 18,000 dangerous offenders already ineligible for the progression model, this Government have excluded rape and serious child sex offences from eligibility for changes to release dates under the Sentencing Act. Unlawful killings, including manslaughter, causing or allowing the death of a child, and death by dangerous driving, are also excluded, as well as indecent assault, ensuring that more historical child sex offences prosecuted under older laws are treated consistently with equivalent offences today. That means that hundreds more dangerous criminals will be staying behind bars for longer, including those who killed PC Andrew Harper in the line of duty.

The first releases on the progression model took place on 1 October, with His Majesty’s Prison and Probation Service working closely with operational partners to ensure that eligible offenders were released safely into the community. As the second tranche of releases begins today, robust arrangements remain in place to manage releases, support probation practitioners and supervising offenders, and ensure that those subject to electronic monitoring requirements are fitted with a tag. As part of the supervision of offenders released into the community, HMPPS will maintain rigorous oversight of those on licence, with measures in place to recall those who are non-compliant.

We recognise the significant effect that release date changes can have on victims. We will ensure that those in the victim contact scheme who are affected by the new exclusions are informed if there are any changes to the release date of the offender in their case. I have also instructed my officials to attempt to contact victims not in that scheme to provide information, should they wish for that to happen. We have launched the victim support offender release helpline, with nearly £19 million of additional funding, to provide victims with emotional support, practical advice such as safety planning, and general information about sentencing changes.

It is important to add that the Minister for Prisons, Probation and Reducing Reoffending is unable to be here today because she is currently speaking with governors about early release and how the implementation of the progression model is going”.
Lord Keen of Elie (Con)

My Lords, when discharging more and more criminals before completion of their prison sentence, one simple measure of public protection would be electronic tagging. We know that the Government have failed to implement this measure, with many of these criminals leaving prison early without a tag. Will the Minister advise how many of the latest cohort of 600 criminals were released without a tag, and will he undertake that any further criminals who are released early will be electronically tagged before they leave prison?
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Ministry of Justice (Lord Lemos) (Lab)

My Lords, we inherited a failing tagging system with record backlogs, but since 2024 we have been working hard to fix this and the install rates are up nearly 50% since then. We are also investing £100 million in electronic monitoring, tagging offenders before releases and strengthening victim protections via new alert systems. All of this helps us to cut the number of unmonitored offenders and protect victims. We are confident that we have enough equipment and Serco field resource to deliver. The situation has improved. Our quarterly electronic monitoring statistics include figures for the number of prison leavers fitted with tags, and the next quarterly update will be published in October.
Lord Foulkes of Cumnock (Lab Co-op)
My Lords—
Baroness Brinton (LD)
Excuse me.
Lord Foulkes of Cumnock (Lab Co-op)
I am really sorry.
Baroness Brinton (LD)

I am grateful to the noble Lord. I want to follow on from the question of the noble and learned Lord, Lord Keen, about tagging. Other countries quite often tag prisoners before they leave or at the prison gates. I want to raise one other global example which worked really well but does not relate to prisoners. Taiwan introduced tagging for people having to isolate at home during Covid very quickly by using local resources, and that worked very successfully. Will the Government undertake to look at both the issue that the noble and learned Lord raised about prisoners being tagged before they leave and innovative ways of making this work across the country?
Lord Lemos (Lab)

The Government will do so, of course. As the noble Baroness and the House will know from discussions around what is now the Sentencing Act, we have introduced a presumption that offenders released early will be tagged. We have a range of tagging options at our disposal: curfew tags, alcohol tags and GPS tags. I am interested in what the noble Baroness said about Taiwan; I did not know about that. None the less, the situation is clear and we all understand it. It was not a good situation with tagging; we are improving it, but it is clearly a central aspect of how we will manage the criminal justice system in the future.
Lord Foulkes of Cumnock (Lab Co-op)

I sincerely apologise to the noble Baroness, Lady Brinton, for jumping the gun. If the party opposite was ever returned to power, it is proposing, I think, to create 50,000 new prison places. As I understand it, in 14 years it created only 500 new prison places and closed 23 prisons. Is the Minister aware of the miracle solution found by the noble and learned Lord, Lord Keen, and his colleagues?
Lord Lemos (Lab)

I believe in miracles—I am a Catholic—but even I think 50,000 is a lot. We are undertaking the largest prison-building programme since the Victorian era. In December 2024, this Government published our plan to create 14,000 additional places. I do not think I have said from the Dispatch Box before that we have already delivered through new prisons the expansion and refurbishment of the existing estate and temporary accommodation amounting to some 3,300 places. We have therefore made a substantial impact on prison place supply. My noble friend is right that under the Conservative Government there was a net increase of only 500 places in 14 years, and indeed they were responsible for closing 23 prisons. As for the 50,000 new places that the leader of the Opposition has promised, seeing will be believing.
Viscount Hailsham (Con)

My Lords, many of us want to know how many newly released prisoners have been tagged, and how many have been returned to prison having committed an offence. We are not getting that information from the Government at the moment. Is the explanation for that failure either that they do not have the information, or that they choose not to give it? If it is the latter, why?
Lord Lemos (Lab)
Neither of those are the explanation. As I have already said, we quarterly release figures both on tagging and on reoffending, and we shall continue to do that. That is the Government’s position.
Lord Pannick (CB)
My Lords, have the Government conducted any assessment of how many additional serious crimes are likely to be committed as a result of the early release scheme?
Lord Lemos (Lab)

It is very early days for the early release scheme, and I want to make one thing clear. There is a great deal of confusion in the public debate about early release schemes. There have been a succession of such schemes under the previous Government, and indeed we in this Government had two early release schemes because there were fewer than 100 prison places. The early release scheme we are now engaged in is part of the earned progression model. This is a new approach to sentencing that came out of the Gauke review, which we discussed at length in the proceedings of what is now the Sentencing Act. This is not just early release to reduce prison numbers; it is a considered policy approach that we put through the Sentencing Act. We have made lots of assessments and debated them, but it is very early days for this new model, and I do not think that the noble Lord would expect me to quote numbers after such a short period of time.
The Lord Bishop of Manchester

My Lords, I declare my interest as a trustee of the Clink Charity. We work both inside and outside prisons, helping prisoners prepare for release. Prisoners now being released under these schemes, often at very short notice, are coming out ill-prepared. I wonder if the Government have made an assessment of what additional preparation needs to be made and how that can be done to allow prisoners to adjust to life outside without reoffending.
Lord Lemos (Lab)

I thank the right reverend Prelate for that question, and I know he has been deeply involved in this area of work. It is not good to disagree with Bishops, but I am going to, if I may. I do not accept the characterisation that people are ill-prepared. In this round of early releases, under the earned progression model, we are releasing people in tranches over 10 phases. During the last early release scheme, which was so urgent, we released more people in only two tranches. We are doing a great deal to prepare people for release, and we are working with the Probation Service. These early releases are much better planned and delivered, and I expect that to have a considerable benefit.
Lord Woodley (Lab)

My Lords, as we are all aware, these early releases are putting huge pressure on the Probation Service, which is suffering badly after the last Government’s failings. The workloads are high, and that is reflected in the resignations. Does the Minister agree that these outstanding public servants should be paid properly for the job that they do, and that we should do everything we can to make sure that their ballot for strike action does not have to take place?
Lord Lemos (Lab)

As I have said from this Dispatch Box many times before, we are asking a lot of probation —and we are asking more under our new model, particularly regarding the second phase of intensive supervision. We have invested £700 million and we are onboarding a number of new probation officers—1,300 this year. On my noble friend’s question, we certainly hope that there will not be industrial action. We are working to reduce the workload of probation officers, and we have committed to achieving that. I do not want to leave your Lordships under any illusion: building a viable Probation Service that is bigger and better than the one we inherited is a key priority in making our new approaches to sentencing effective.
Lord Clarke of Nottingham (Con)

My Lords, the main cause of the present prison crisis has been Governments of all parties over the past 30 years trying to prove they are tough on crime by encouraging the sentencing of ever more people to prison for longer and longer periods. I think we now have the highest incarceration rate in Europe, and the average sentence is about double what it was when I was Justice Secretary 30 years ago—and it is probably more than that compared with the distant past when I practised at the criminal Bar. The Government are now going to build more prisons. If they insist on doing that, could they use the space in the prisons to devote more time to rehabilitation? The public will be better served if we put more effort into—and had more space in which to put the effort—reducing reoffending when prisoners are released, so that we have fewer victims of future crime. Meanwhile, despite our policy, the rate of serious crime in this country has never been lower. It has been falling for the last 30 years, as it also has in countries that have reduced their sentencing policies, such as the Netherlands.
Lord Lemos (Lab)

I entirely agree with the noble Lord about the way in which sentence lengths have increased. That is why we made the changes we did in the Sentencing Act. He is absolutely right to say that there is no evidence that that has any direct correlation with the rates of crime or, importantly, the public perception of crime. As a novice and amateur politician, I have to say that assumptions that legislating for longer sentences on the basis

title: Housing: National Targets
contributions: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (Baroness Taylor of Stevenage) (Lab)

My Lords, our devolution reforms will give mayors and strategic authorities greater powers to support housing delivery within a national framework, enabling them to direct housing investment to reflect their local housing needs. Housing targets are an important tool to make sure that sufficient housing is delivered in the right places, and the Government have no plans to amend the standard method for assessing housing need introduced in December 2024.
Lord Evans of Guisborough (Con)

My Lords, I am grateful to the Minister for her helpful response. Not all of us share her optimism, unfortunately. As a former deputy mayor of London, I was disappointed to learn that Taylor Wimpey, a major housebuilding developer, recently pulled out of any further projects in London. Its chief executive stated as an explanation that: “The reward for undertaking … development in London has … evaporated”. Does the Minister share my concern? How does she expect the Government, who have promised affordable housing to buy and to rent, to provide housing when they are making it unaffordable to build?
Baroness Taylor of Stevenage (Lab)

It is not this Government who are making housing unaffordable to build. There are a number of factors affecting that. But I accept that there is an urgent need for more housing, especially social and affordable housing and particularly in London. That is why we are acting to address this. In March, the Government and the Greater London Authority confirmed a package of temporary emergency measures providing targeted support for housebuilders to improve the viability that the noble Lord spoke of and to get quicker approvals for new housing schemes. We are also making major longer-term investment, including in the social and affordable homes programme that I have spoken about many times in this Chamber, with up to £11.7 billion for London and £1.5 billion from the new low-interest loans scheme for social and affordable housing.
The Lord Speaker (Lord Forsyth of Drumlean)
My Lords, the noble Lord, Lord Campbell-Savours, is taking part remotely. I invite the noble Lord to speak.
Lord Campbell-Savours (Lab) [V]

My Lords, under the devolution Act, mayors have new powers to unlock land for housing. Can we go further by giving local authorities and mayors the ability to reach housing targets through the acquisition of land for housing at agricultural prices, as in the case of the housing development zones in Nijmegen in Holland and Hammarby in Sweden, which I have raised repeatedly in the House? We need some new, radical thinking.
Baroness Taylor of Stevenage (Lab)

My noble friend has indeed raised land supply many times. The English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act strengthens mayoral housing and planning powers, including powers relating to planning applications of potential strategic importance, mayoral development orders and a mayoral community infrastructure levy. Alongside the Planning and Infrastructure Act, it also supports the new framework for spatial development strategies. We continue to look at issues around land supply and at creative and innovative ideas. We continue to look across Europe and elsewhere for ways in which we might help our mayors and leaders to develop on the land that they need to develop.
Baroness Uddin (Non-Afl)

My Lords, I welcome this shift to local government deciding what the housing needs are. I live in Tower Hamlets, where there are about 28,000 people on the social housing waiting list. How will the Government’s designation of data centres as critical national infrastructure affect housing decisions? I hope Ministers will ensure that the proposed data centre in Brick Lane is not built, because it would impact the mass housing crisis and the well-being of children and families.
Baroness Taylor of Stevenage (Lab)

It is very important across the planning system. The noble Baroness raises the important issue of how we balance the needs of our economic infrastructure, of which data centres are an increasingly important part. We just had a whole debate on AI. We cannot operate AI without data centres. That needs to be balanced with the need for housing, and this Government are committed to a streamlined planning system that is plan led, pro-growth, accessible and understandable to all, and delivers that balance as far as possible. We work with our colleagues in Defra on the land use framework to make sure that we take account of all the needs for land.
Baroness Thornhill (LD)

My Lords, currently, Whitehall sets the targets, mayors determine the strategy and planning officers at a very local level take even more decisions under delegated powers. Can the Minister explain exactly what is left for locally elected councillors to determine? How is this felt to strengthen local democracy in the eyes of the local community? That is where the tension at the heart of the noble Lord’s Question originates.
Baroness Taylor of Stevenage (Lab)

I think it was clear that the previous system of not having housing targets was not delivering the housing that we need. We continue to think that the best way for councillors and communities to engage in the development process for their areas is through the local plan process, which will be agreed by the council. We are not changing the consultation rules on planning applications. Representations are considered by the decision-maker, whether that is an officer taking the decision or a planning committee. It is vital that in exercising that democratic oversight planning committees operate as effectively as possible, focusing on applications that require member input while placing trust in skilled planning officers in local authorities and making sure that they decide applications more quickly in the service of residents and businesses.
Lord Bailey of Paddington (Con)

My Lords, if we take London as an example, the Mayor of London has failed to deliver housing over a 10-year period. Which powers will the Government retain to make sure that local authorities and mayors build the homes we need? Do not devolve this power and devolve the responsibility along with it.
Baroness Taylor of Stevenage (Lab)

I have already set out the steps the Government are taking to work with colleagues in London to accelerate housebuilding there. There has already been a significant increase in applications. Through the City Hall Developer Investment Fund and the new homes accelerator, we are providing support to accelerate stalled schemes and driving housing-led regeneration on nationally significant sites, such as Euston. We continue to make sure that we work with the mayor’s office to deliver the housing that London needs.
Lord Best (CB)

My Lords, can I ask the Minister about the devolution to mayors and combined authorities of the power to set up development corporations? These have huge potential, such as the London Legacy Development Corporation. They are going to be really great, but they will need some seed corn—some setting-up funding. Will the Government provide that so that we can see more of these wonderful development corporations?
Baroness Taylor of Stevenage (Lab)

The noble Lord will be aware that I am a big fan of development corporations. We have had many discussions about them. He is quite right that there is some need for capacity. In August, the Prime Minister announced measures to strengthen the capacity and capability of mayoral strategic authorities as part of the Government’s wider devolution agenda, with measures such as Civil Service secondments to mayoral offices, a place-based fast stream pilot, support for digital and data capability and the expansion of leadership development opportunities between central and local government. It is very important that we support areas such as Liverpool. I went to a meeting there recently about its mayoral development corporation, which is doing very exciting work delivering 17,500 homes and 5 million square feet of commercial space. We need to give it every support in the capacity to deliver that.
Baroness O'Neill of Bexley (Con)
The London Borough of Lewisham has estimated that these regulations will increase build costs by 15%. What are the Government doing to cut the costs of building and buying a home?
Baroness Taylor of Stevenage (Lab)

We continue to work with people across the construction sector to look at the issues, but we do not want to go through another Grenfell or have issues around poor-quality build in future. Again, this is an issue of balance. We must absolutely get the balance right and introduce the regulation we need to make sure that people’s homes are safe, affordable and warm and that we do not have the sort of disasters we have seen in the past. Affordability is very much part of that equation, and this is all about balance.
Lord Sahota (Lab)
My Lords, do the Government have any policy to counter land banking by large companies?
Baroness Taylor of Stevenage (Lab)

We have looked extensively at how we urge building to take place. We now have our homes accelerator, which is helping to move forward some sites where development has stalled. I am sure that will contribute to delivering the housing that we all want to see. There is a focus right across our department and the team to make sure that we have taken steps on planning and regulation. We are now moving into the delivery phase, and we have already seen a 15% increase in starts this year.

title: Havant Thicket Reservoir: Pollutants
contributions: Captain of the Honourable Corps of Gentlemen-at-Arms and Chief Whip (Lord Kennedy of Southwark) (Lab Co-op)

My Lords, before the noble Baroness asks her Question, I remind the House that the first supplementary question should take no more than 45 seconds, remaining questions should each take no more than 30 seconds and responses should be of similar length.
Baroness Jones of Moulsecoomb (GP)
I beg leave to ask the Question standing in my name on the Order Paper and deeply resent that. I am one of the shortest speakers in the House.
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Baroness Hayman of Ullock) (Lab)

My Lords, I do not think that the Chief Whip’s comments were personally meant. Reservoir operations must comply with water framework directive objectives. Water companies are required to follow the drinking water safety planning approach and must assess risks to drinking water from the water source that it is taken from until it reaches consumers at the taps. The planned raw water sources to supply the Havant Thicket reservoir have been monitored and mitigations have been proposed where required, including for emerging substances.
Baroness Jones of Moulsecoomb (GP)

I thank the Minister for her Answer, but I am deeply unsatisfied with it, because I assume that it is Southern Water itself that has monitored and checked the sewage effluent that is going to be put into Havant Thicket reservoir. We need a reservoir. We desperately need more water sources, but we cannot trust Southern Water to audit its own discharges. Can the Government do what is being done in countries such as Singapore and create an expert panel to audit exactly what is going into that water supply? The forever chemicals that I have referred to are highly poisonous and pernicious.
Baroness Hayman of Ullock (Lab)

The noble Baroness mentioned Singapore. It is important to say that water recycling is used widely around the world, not just in Singapore but in Australia, the USA and in Belgium. Southern Water is one of the companies that are developing water recycling plants for the future. It is also important to say that the project is going to use highly treated recycled water that has been through a series of very strict treatment and quality checks before it would enter the Havant Thicket reservoir. Water stored in the reservoir would then go through further treatment and testing before being supplied as drinking water. I am happy for the noble Baroness to raise with me specific concerns around Southern Water after this Question.
Baroness Finlay of Llandaff (CB)

Following Michael Sheen’s documentary showing that polychlorinated biphenyls are dumped at 14 sites across the UK, some of which are near Newport and Cardiff, what action are the Government taking to detect high levels of contamination both in drinking water and in farm produce?
Baroness Hayman of Ullock (Lab)

The Environment Agency works closely with a range of UK and international bodies to understand the different sources, because it is important that we understand where PFAS are coming from so we can have a proper risk-based approach to assessing and managing risks. That work is helping to inform the design requirements for additional water treatment schemes such as the one that we are discussing. Defra has made a commitment to protect public health and the environment while supporting innovation and economic growth. This is part of how we are going to work together to manage PFAS contamination.
Baroness McIntosh of Pickering (Con)

My Lords, not only should reservoirs be clean but they should ideally be full. Last week, on Friday, Yorkshire officially entered a drought status due to low water levels in reservoirs and rivers. I know the noble Baroness believes that there should be more reservoirs, particularly more smaller reservoirs, so what can she and her department do to remove the barriers to more smaller reservoirs being built?
Baroness Hayman of Ullock (Lab)

The noble Baroness makes a really important point, and this year’s drought has demonstrated that we need better ways in which we can hold water, particularly on farm, so that we can manage resilience of food security. Defra is very cognisant of this. We are working hard with the farmers’ union, for example, around what we can do to increase food security. Obviously, holding water on farm is part of that.
Baroness Grender (LD)

My Lords, does the Minister accept that some of the underlying issues in this Oral Question are precisely why we need the long-promised clean water Bill, or whatever it is now going to be called, including urgent statutory protection for chalk streams? What immediate safeguards will apply before that legislation arrives? She expressed a lot of urgency about that previously. And when will the Bill be published?
Baroness Hayman of Ullock (Lab)

I cannot give the noble Baroness a date for when the Bill is coming, but it is something that we are working on very hard at the moment, because it is important that we bring it forward. We know there is a lot of anticipation around it, but it is also a very important Bill. The noble Baroness mentioned chalk streams. Building reservoirs is an important part of how we protect chalk streams. We need to stop the amount of abstraction that is taking place. Reservoir building is important if we are to reduce the need to take water from very sensitive environments.
Lord Watts (Lab)
My Lords, is it not the case that farmers and golfers use a lot of water inefficiently? Do we not need to do more to encourage them to be more effective?
Baroness Hayman of Ullock (Lab)

One of the really difficult questions around drought is who has access to water. Golf courses use an enormous amount of water, and there were some issues with some water companies and golf courses earlier this year. It is really an issue for the water companies and industry to sort among themselves, but, clearly, if there is a particular issue, government will step in.
Lord Grayling (Con)

Will the Minister accept that if our system for supporting agriculture was adjusted so that there was a proper biodiversity margin between agricultural land and rivers, we would significantly reduce the amount of effluent flowing from that land into rivers and improve river quality?
Baroness Hayman of Ullock (Lab)

I totally agree with the noble Lord, because that is something I have done myself through a catchment-sensitive farming grant. You can get grants like that. We fenced off our river to stop the cattle going down to it, to stop that kind of pollution going in, and we planted alongside it to, again, stop that pollution. You can get catchment-sensitive grants to look at things like that, and it is important that we encourage people to apply for them.
Baroness Miller of Chilthorne Domer (LD)

My Lords, that is a sticking plaster for as long as we are mixing industrial waste into sewage waste so that the PFAS are still coming through into the water in the runoff from the fields. What would the Minister say to that?
Baroness Hayman of Ullock (Lab)

Clearly, we need to resolve the pollution of PFAS into our waterways and streams as much as we can. The Government have brought forward a strategy around PFAS; we have to look at how we tackle this. We are also looking at the best ways of monitoring and at the sources, because if we do not fully understand where they are coming from, we cannot fully tackle it. But we are working hard in Defra to manage that.
Lord Blencathra (Con)

My Lords, I begin by stating that I have deep respect for the noble Baroness, Lady Jones of Moulsecoomb, however long she speaks. For about 40 years, she has campaigned dutifully for mainstream green and environmental issues, and sometimes I have found myself in agreement with her. However, I must say that I have nothing but contempt for the current Green Party leader, who is a despicable piece of work and not fit to have any role in public life in this country. I have a question on regulations for the Minister—a simple one. Our current regulatory framework is too fragmented, and our regulators too unaccountable, to deal effectively with the issues raised today, as we have all seen with the Environment Agency and its failure to stop massive rubbish dumps in protected landscapes. What are the Government doing to review Defra’s 34 arm’s-length bodies—as we are proposing—to bring infrastructure, project delivery and nature recovery under more direct ministerial control?
Baroness Hayman of Ullock (Lab)

I am sure that the noble Lord is aware, as will be many noble Lords, that we carried out the Corry review to look at how the different arm’s-length bodies in Defra work, not just in the water industry but across the board. We need to work better, to stop things falling through the cracks and to make sure that regulators do what we want them to do and what they need to do. It should not always be focused just on finances; environment should also be taken into account, and we are working hard to make things more efficient and effective.
Baroness Jones of Moulsecoomb (GP)
