My Lords, first, I would like the noble Lord, Lord Blencathra, to withdraw half of his comments in Hansard . I say to the Minister that I still have not heard a way forward on this. These chemicals are highly dangerous, and there is no regulation to cover them at the moment. I repeat that we cannot trust Southern Water. Its Budds Farm wastewater treatment works was found in research conducted by the Marine Conservation Society to be releasing forever chemicals into the environment via treated effluent. We cannot keep allowing this. We have to put in regulation.
Baroness Hayman of Ullock (Lab)

There are two things that I would say to the noble Baroness. First, as she said, the scheme is going to take treated wastewater from Budds Farm wastewater treatment works. It will purify it to a high standard at a new water recycling plant before it is transferred to the reservoir. The water stored in the reservoir will subsequently be abstracted and conveyed to the Otterbourne water supply works for treatment and supply to customers. That would create a new drought-resilient source of water for the wider region, which is desperately needed. Secondly, we are asked all the time, “Why it is taking you so long to build reservoirs? Why have you not started one of the new nine reservoirs that you want? When are you going to complete it? Why has it been delayed?” Part of the reason we have a problem building new reservoirs in this country is that when we try, nobody wants them.

title: UK and Poland:  Security and Defence Partnership
contributions: Lord Johnson of Lainston (Con)

My Lords, I am particularly delighted that we are having this debate on the day that President Zelensky is in London meeting the Prime Minister, I think while we are having this discussion. That only highlights the importance of agreements such as this. We are going to scrutinise the UK-Poland Security and Defence Partnership and our International Agreements Committee’s report on that agreement. The agreement was signed in May 2026. The then Prime Minister described it—this is an important statement—as “the biggest step forward in our defence and security relationship with Poland in a generation”. It establishes a framework for co-operation between the UK and Poland across foreign policy, defence and security, and a whole range of other areas. The scrutiny period under CRaG expired on 9 September. We reported the agreement to the House for special attention and debate in the light of its political significance, but, in the light of our overall conclusions, we did not think it was necessary for this debate to take place during the CRaG period. I thank the Government for their decision to publish the treaty online ahead of its formal laying in Parliament, which gave us more time to take evidence and therefore produce this more comprehensive report. I would be very grateful if the Minister could feed back to his colleagues that that practice is extremely welcome, particularly for treaties such as this. It gives us more time and does not necessitate asking for an extension to the CRaG process. The outcome is eminently satisfactory. I thank the witnesses, who were numerous, especially and including the Minister for Europe and senior officials from the FCDO and the MoD. I thank the staff who support our committee, admirably led by Dom Walsh, in particular Priscilla Tomaz for her support in leading our inquiry and, effectively, producing the report. I think we can all agree that the UK and Poland are entering into this treaty at a time of sustained geopolitical challenge, in particular Russia’s war in Ukraine and the growth of hybrid threats. In this context, we agree with the Government that Poland is clearly a vital partner and ally on NATO’s eastern flank. As the treaty recognises, Poland plays an increasingly central role in the Euro-Atlantic security architecture and in shaping European responses to Russian aggression. Committee Members will be aware that this is not the first defence treaty that the UK and Poland have signed. It aims to build on a previous defence treaty from 2017 and a non-binding declaration signed in 2023. However, compared with its predecessors, this treaty takes a far more expansive approach to the issues that are considered relevant to defence and security, including economic resilience, energy and climate security, and tackling illegal migration. This expansive approach reflects the increasingly diverse threats that the UK and Poland face. However, the committee was concerned that it would cause challenges in co-ordinating collaboration across departments. I am not saying this as a political point, but I think that getting departments to work together is often a challenge even within His Majesty’s Government. To multiply that by the cubic number of two to add a second country’s government departments to collaborate will represent a significant challenge. I would be very grateful for the Minister’s comments on that, in the sense of the steps the Government will take to ensure that we truly have an integrated approach to implementing this treaty. In the current security context, the treaty strengthens our bilateral defence relationship with Poland and affirms the importance of co-operation at this time of great uncertainty. By expanding the scope of co-operation beyond traditional defence policy issues, it establishes a comprehensive framework to address the increasingly integrated nature of the threats that face both the UK and Poland. These hybrid threats include provisions on collaboration in cyber security, critical infrastructure, supply chain resilience, and so on. This is particularly valuable for private defence companies, which are often the first targets of hybrid attacks. I think the committee was pleased to note the element of industrial co-operation, where the treaty aims to make the UK and Poland joint European leaders in complex weapons manufacturing. As it happens, I spoke today to BAE Systems, which wanted me to express its support for this treaty because it pushed further the collaboration between BAE Systems and PGZ and enabled a far more institutional approach to combined weapons development and delivery. That is an important win for the UK defence industry and clearly a good thing for both countries. The question that comes from this—this is the theme that the committee wishes to raise in scrutinising this treaty—is: can we be sure that the Ministry of Defence will dedicate the right level of resourcing to the teams behind these projects? If it does not do that, it will not succeed. For the benefit of other Members taking part in this debate, these processes are not simply about single weapons development—this is the important point. We want to see us move from single-platform development collaboration to overall defence collaborations, as we saw with BAE Systems in Norway. I am sure there will be some well-phrased words from the Minister on that, but we would quite like to hear some concrete responses to those points. This leads on to the point that much of the treaty is very high level and general, rather than setting out detailed, substantive obligations. The Minister for Europe told us that this was deliberate and designed to allow for greater flexibility. Alongside this treaty is a list of 14 landmark projects, which we hope will turn the ambitions set out in the treaty into tangible outcomes. However, many of those also lack specific timelines and do not outline specific deliverables. We are also concerned about how the treaty’s commitments will be funded. Frankly, someone may say that this is the elephant in the room, in the light of the UK’s defence spending plans and whether the UK’s broader commitments to NATO on defence spending will be met. The uncertainty around our defence spending plans undermines the UK’s reputation as an ally at a time of geopolitical uncertainty. Clearly, Poland will respond positively to this treaty from its point of view only if it feels that we are investing enough capital, time and resources into our entire defence industry, and then the specific treaty obligations that we have with it. I am sure the Minister cannot give me anything significantly specific about our defence spending plans, but it will be very important, since I am sure the Polish military will be listening to this debate—as, no doubt, are many other people as well—to underline truly our financial commitment to defence in general and to this project specifically. I will move on to one of the other points that were raised by the committee in our inquiry. Article 2 of the treaty provides that the parties “reaffirm their commitment to NATO as the foundation of their collective defence, and to their obligations … in the North Atlantic Treaty … in particular Article 5”. It then states that in the event of an armed attack against the other party, the parties “shall assist one another, including by military means in accordance with Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty”. We clearly welcome this reaffirmation of both parties’ commitment to NATO but we were a bit unclear as to whether the treaty adds commitments that go beyond our NATO commitments. The wording of Article 2 of the treaty, which states that assistance by “military means” is to be in accordance with Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, appears to suggest that any use of military force in response to an armed attack would take place within the NATO framework. However, can the Minister clarify whether Article 2 creates any mutual defence commitments in addition to those under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty? The EM notes that the devolved Administrations were consulted, but added that “there are limited implications for the Devolved Administrations”. I know, from having been in the Minister’s position, that that is understandable, given the complication of trying to get the approval of the devolved Administrations, particularly in a reserved matter such as the creation of treaties. However, this treaty specifically goes beyond simple military matters, and by its very nature, if it is to be effective, it covers whole areas of home affairs—immigration, crime, and so on. We really would like to understand from the Minister that the devolved Administrations have been properly consulted and that they are aware of their commitments that might relate to this treaty. All of them are important and I am sure they are all shared goals, but that has not been clearly enough indicated. There was no reference to the treaty’s provisions for amendment or the scrutiny implications. We have repeatedly asked that the Government should say more in the Explanatory Memorandum on which amendments will be subject to ratification and, therefore, scrutiny. This is the third consecutive report—if the Minister could note this—in which we have had to make this point. It is very important that Parliament has the opportunity to scrutinise further amendments of these treaties. Many of them are designed to be flexible in the modern world, which we support, but we must ensure that we have effective oversight. In conclusion, I believe personally, and I believe this is the strong view of the committee, that this treaty is to be welcomed. It enhances bilateral co-operation with a very important ally at what is clearly a highly challenging time and contains some important provisions, especially the principle of an expanded mandate between the two countries, important defence sharing and support for our industrial base. However, it is high level and general in nature. It remains to be seen how co-operation will be advanced in practice and, importantly, how it is to be paid for. It therefore remains to be seen what its true long-term significance will be. I look forward to the Minister’s comments, and I beg to move.
Lord Hannay of Chiswick (CB)

My Lords, the security agreement between the UK and Poland, which we are debating and which has been so ably introduced by our chair, the noble Lord, Lord Johnson, has been firmly supported by your Lordships’ International Agreements Committee, of which I have the honour to be a member. I hope that this support will receive backing in this debate, enabling the agreement to go forward for early ratification. The agreement is an ancillary one, in the sense that both parties to it are firm members of the Atlantic alliance and committed by Article 5 of the NATO treaty to come to the collective defence of its members if one or several of them are attacked. From all the evidence we took on this agreement, there was no suggestion that the Article 5 commitment is undermined or contradicted, or that there risks being confusion of responsibility as a result of it. What is lacking in the agreement, however, is any real degree of specificity—the chair of our committee made that point several times during his speech. There was no specificity about how the parties to it will put flesh on the bones of their broad commitments. That remains to be defined and to be effected. That it should be so in a meaningful and operationally convincing way is essential if the agreement is not to remain just words on paper. I would be grateful if the Minister, in replying to this debate, could give an assurance that this follow-up is already in hand and under way. Yesterday, the Warsaw Security Forum met. The Foreign Secretary was present at it and presumably had a good deal to say on matters that were relevant to this agreement—as others there would have, such as the Norwegian Foreign Minister, the German Foreign Minister and, of course, the Polish Foreign Minister. I would be grateful if the Minister could give us some sense of how that meeting went and where it took matters to. Another essential feature is that an agreement such as this has to enjoy wholehearted cross-party support. Without that, its implementation will always be at risk. Judging from this debate, that cross-party support would seem to be assured in this country. We were told in our sessions with witnesses that that would seem to be the case in Poland too. Does that correspond to the Government’s information? Perhaps the Minister could give us a word or two on that. It is sometimes said that those who ignore or overlook history are fated to repeat it. Well, Anglo-Polish security co-operation is not an empty book. In 1939, this country gave Poland a firm guarantee of support in the event of an attack. We were then unable to validate that following the Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and the aggression against Poland and the Baltic states comm

title: Food Security
contributions: Baroness Teather (LD)

My Lords, it is a huge privilege to open this debate. Food security is incredibly complex. Addressing it has also never been more pressing. We now face multiple global threats that could create profound food shocks—shocks that will fall unequally on our population. The question is how we can best prepare as a nation and make our food system more resilient. Planning effective interventions on food security requires us to think systemically across silos—from farming and the environment to foreign and defence policy, international trade, public health, local government, planning regulations, business logistics, behavioural science and much more besides. I am certainly no expert in all these areas, but one thing I have learnt as a new Member is that breadth of expertise is something this House has in spades. I suggested this title for debate because this kind of urgent, vital and knotty challenge plays to the strengths of the House. I am grateful to noble Lords who have given their time and experience to participate, and I look forward to hearing what they have to say. As the topic is huge, I want to focus my remarks on three areas: first, the threats to our food system and our national response; secondly, efforts to build resilience for the longer term; and thirdly, the need to involve the whole of society in the effort. Multiple reports in recent years have warned that the UK is dangerously unprepared for potentially catastrophic shocks to our food system. Professor Tim Lang’s impressive report for the National Preparedness Commission last year paints a comprehensive picture of current vulnerabilities. The National Audit Office warned last month that the sector’s ability to withstand events has not been tested. Farmers tell us that climate change is already a reality, creating huge unpredictability. Crops this year have been affected by drought, flooding, excessive rain and extreme heat, which of course has sometimes made it too hot to harvest. While some yields have held up, we have seen the worst cereal harvest on record, and with a supercharged El Niño, it is only likely to get worse. The Joint Intelligence Committee has given stark warnings about the potential for the collapse of ecosystems within five years and the threat to national security and food supply. In addition, there are new crises emerging. Attacks on international shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have sharply increased the cost of diesel and fertiliser for UK farmers, and threaten critical shortages in Africa and Asia, from which we import. Of course, Hormuz is not the only international choke point we should worry about. We have seen cyber attacks on supermarkets and distributors. This week, the director-general of MI5 warned about the risk of AI-enabled drone attacks on UK soil, a real concern when almost 95% of retail food moves through just 131 distribution centres. In this new reality, it is naive to assume that private sector switching of supply chains alone will be enough to keep food flowing. It is certainly the case that supermarkets responded with impressive speed to maintain supplies during Covid, but Covid also exposed structural failings in our system, which we have not yet addressed. First, adequate food supply does not equate to all the people being fed. The Food Foundation estimates that one in eight households are already food insecure. I saw during Covid, while I was running a charity for people facing destitution, that global food shocks fall unequally and can have devastating health impacts. Secondly, none of the national food security assessments considers how the public might actually behave in a food shock scenario. The flipside of highly optimised, just-in-time logistics is that very small changes in consumer behaviour can quickly empty shelves. Thirdly, the same efficient logistics have all but eliminated the need for storage. We could have just a few days of food available in the face of a catastrophic interruption to supply. We import around 40% of our food and more than 80% of our fruit. It is vital that we increase the proportion of food that we grow in the UK, but this is only part of the story. Food ingredients are often passed along lengthy, tortuous supply chains before they end up on the plate, with processing, manufacturing and distribution happening in different locations. Disruptions anywhere can cascade and amplify along the route. Given this context, our national assessment of risk looks dangerously complacent. The national risk register, for example, has very little on the food system and, where it does consider food, the focus is on risk of contamination rather than interruptions to supply or access. So, what is needed? First, the Cabinet Office frankly needs to up its game and update the way in which we assess and think about food security in the light of the new threats. We need a special national risk register study that includes consideration of public reactions and dynamics. Secondly, the Government’s post-implementation review of the Civil Contingencies Act provides an opportunity to integrate food resilience and to think about the kinds of structures that we need at local and regional level to co-ordinate efforts. Local areas need plans to get food to the vulnerable and an understanding of community assets and networks that could help. We also need a more grown-up conversation with the public than a website telling people to stock up on tins. Thirdly, while there are legal duties to ensure that food is safe, there are no duties to ensure that everyone gets fed. It really is not clear who would hold responsibility for this in a crisis. Finally, we need a rapid assessment of what storage is available at national, regional and local levels and a plan to improve it. This is not an easy fix. Can the Government convene a cross-sector taskforce, for example, to wrestle with it? Other countries, everywhere from Switzerland to China, have national stores and many European nations are developing plans to store food. A key theme from Professor Lang’s report for the National Preparedness Commission was the need to move our peacetime food system to a more distributed and diverse model, to boost domestic production and to enhance regional food systems. The UK is unusual in having an underdeveloped regional food system compared with, say, France or Italy. Long-term sustainability in our food system depends on protecting the natural resources that farming depends on—soil health and biodiversity—and transitioning from reliance on globally imported fertiliser. Yesterday, the Government published a new Organic Action Plan for England, to boost the share of food farmed organically. My first reading of it suggests that there is much in it that is welcome, including backing organic farming to boost resilience to climate change. We have to support farmers to transition to new ways of farming. That means backing those willing to experiment with organic and regenerative farming models that focus on soil health and are not tied to inorganic fertilisers. We must fund rigorous scientific research into crop yields, soil, nature and profitability and share those lessons widely. However, the new organic plan also leaves lots of questions. There has been exasperation from farmers at the chaos of the sustainable farming incentive scheme. Small growers told me that, even if the scheme had been well managed, it left them out by design. They are a critical component of a regional food system and often already farming in sustainable ways. For example, Vallis Veg in Somerset, an established small farm, told me that the economics of the food system currently relies on farmers in effect exploiting themselves. Its owners are deeply committed to agroecological farming but do not have the resources to certify as organic, which the organic action plan acknowledges is a problem. Vallis Veg’s commitment to the cause extends to supporting new entrants. It provides a small plot of land for free to a local grower to run a market garden, who is allowed to live on site for below-market rent, but even with all that generosity he struggles to make a living. According to a recent McCain Foods survey, one in four farmers made a loss or barely broke even in the past year, and two in five considered quitting farming altogether. We know that those financial pressures are particularly acute for small farmers. Those who make it work often rely on additional funding streams. The inspirational Prospects Trust on the Cambridge-Suffolk border includes an accessible nature reserve, organic farm, shop and retail outlet and provides placements for people with learning disabilities or autism, funded through social care. It employs 51 local people part time and grows delicious fruit and veg. Over decades, it has built trusted relationships with a local organic wholesaler and a Cambridge college chef willing to cook veg that it cannot sell elsewhere, reducing food waste. It told me that relationships are key to its ability to adapt to shifting weather, because constant communication allows it to agree with the customer on what it can crop. It is a remarkable success story, but there was frustration that it could not access the agricultural water resilience grant to replace its leaky irrigation system because it could not quickly raise the 50% capital contribution needed. Can the Minister say what the Government will do to support small farms such as these? Incidentally, Cambridge is an example of a city with a vibrant local food partnership, much enthusiasm and fertile arable land. But without capital investment in the missing middle of infrastructure on storage and distribution, it is difficult to turn ambition into a functioning regional food system. The founder of the fledgling Cambridge Food Hub has been trying to secure investment for that missing middle for 13 years. He illustrated the problem that he is seeking to fix by explaining that, even though one of the largest strawberry farmers in the country is based just outside the city, local businesses must buy their produce from New Covent Garden Market. That means that fruit grown six miles away must travel 120 miles—Cambridge to London and then back to Cambridge—in a refrigerated lorry. That is madness. It is worth contrasting that with the success of the Welsh Veg in Schools initiative. With Welsh Government backing, Food Sense Wales to broker deals and local infrastructure donated by Castell Howell, local growers have been able to co-ordinate what they grow. More veg is being grown and local farms now supply over half of Wales’s councils. The new organic action plan restates the Government’s ambitions to use public sector procurement to support domestic growing and it references Sustain’s Bridging the Gap programme, but it is short on detail about how the Government will invest in the so-called missing middle infrastructure to make regional food systems fly. Will the Minister tell me what plans her department has to make good on Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledge to boost local food procurement? The final theme that I want to touch on is how we can ensure that our efforts on food security involve the whole of society. We have a long-standing problem with food inequality and it is getting worse. The Government announced small pots of funding for the Good Food Neighbourhoods programme to tackle fruit and veg deserts, but what is missing is a coherent national strategy with teeth that draws together public health, planning policy, housing strategies, local government, agricultural policy and public attitudes. Now is the moment for a good food Bill—something that covers the full arc of the food system, allowing co-ordinated decision-making at national and local levels. It would allow us to set targets on childhood obesity, food security and domestic production and would provide certainty about the direction of travel for farmers, businesses, investors and consumers. It would also kick-start a consultation about what we mean when we talk about a healthy nutritious sustainable diet. What would a reference diet look like? What implications would it have for our agricultural strategy? What needs to shift in public attitudes if we are to consume more of the foods that we can grow here, such as beans and pulses? A consensus on these elements would guide policy-making priorities in peacetime, but it would also be critical in an emergency. Joined-up policy-making would also give more creative projects a chance, such as peri-urban growing and land for community gardens and allotments. No one is arguing that community growing projects will fill the gap in domestic production, but what it can do is build solidarity, narrow the distance between farmers and urban populations, build knowledge and shape attitudes to what we eat and cook. In the end, in an emergency, it is only communities acting together that can provide civil resilience. Everything we do now to invest

title: Support for Family Businesses
contributions: Baroness in Waiting/Government Whip (Baroness Dacres of Lewisham) (Lab)
My Lords, this debate should take one hour. I remind your Lordships to keep to time, as that is very precious today.
Lord Cameron of Dillington (CB)

My Lords, I must first declare that I am a member of a Somerset farming family, albeit now retired and living in Cornwall. I have also in my time started various small businesses, some of which failed but some did not. There are those who view entrepreneurial capitalism in a very bad light. They associate it with large, faceless corporations who pay the minimum of wages, treat their staff badly and ensure that the directors and shareholders take as much money out of the company as possible in as quick a time as possible, but, of course, there are almost no companies like this, and if there were they would not last long. Nevertheless, it is true that both the stock market and the Treasury are most interested in those businesses that give the largest possible financial returns. The Treasury even gives the impression that small businesses are expendable and that their long-term survival through the generations is not relevant to the nation’s economic growth. But these family businesses are the seed corn of our future economic growth. They are our best hope and produce a range of wider benefits that are not recognised by the markets or policymakers. I remember Gordon Brown saying to me that new Labour was all about encouraging greater economic growth but getting the businesses involved to give back more to society. That is almost exactly what family businesses do. They are likely to treat their staff as family and even their customers as such. The business’s reputation is their reputation and often they will go beyond the call of duty to protect it. Think of the voluntary work that these families put into their community, through local Round Tables, Rotary clubs, or serving on local charities or councils. They are the pillars that make their community a community. They are immensely hard-working. In my rural world, if you add up all the hours put into the farming or family business by the family, including the children, it is possible that they are working for less than the minimum wage, as a whole. These family businesses make up 93% of all UK businesses. They generate trillions of pounds of turnover and provide 57% of private sector employment—some 15.8 million employees. They contribute £425 billion per annum to the UK Exchequer. They drive innovation, employment and, as I have said, community stability. We really are a nation of shopkeepers, in its widest sense, which now includes highly technical businesses at the cutting edge of their fields, harnessing the science and research that the nation also excels at. Family enterprises are the lifeblood of our nation, more so than most of our competitors; some employ fewer than five people and some employ thousands. On how we enable more of the former to become the latter, our financial success as a country depends. So, what do we have to do? First, we have to stop looking at these hard-working families as a go-to place to find money whenever the Chancellor needs more funds for triple-lock pensions or ever more generous social services. Many of these family businesses have minimal spare revenue available even if, over the years and generations—by dint of borrowing and sheer hard work—they have built up considerable capital assets in their business, most of which have been paid for out of income already taxed. The Government must also stop imposing extra costs on these businesses. They almost all say that they would employ more non-family staff if they did not cost so much. In 2020, employing a 21 year-old cost £17,000 per annum, but now, in 2026, owing to minimum wage changes, it costs £29,600 per annum. No small business can afford to employ an untrained 21 year-old at that price, so who loses? The 21 year-old NEETs lose, of course. Their lives become hopeless, just when they should be setting out on their careers. The other loser is the Treasury, because it now has to pay benefits to these unemployed 21 year-olds, as opposed to receiving their lifelong payments of tax. What else can we do? Training and access to capital are two areas for improvement that are best served locally. The self-employed, particularly the young—my knowledge comes from the rural young—are happy to pay for training in simple stuff, such as drawing up budgets, cash flows and marketing campaigns, which are really important if you want to earn your own money by mending bikes, motorbikes or computers, or fitting routers into houses and businesses, or just cleaning windows. I know that it sounds like small fry from the Treasury’s point of view, but helping the next generation to pay taxes rather than draw the dole must make a difference. Who knows? Some may one day turn into one of the 300 or so UK family businesses with turnovers in excess of £500 million; but they would all have started small. The other great stumbling block for these businesses is when they need capital to expand, employ more staff, buy new equipment and so on. Unless they have the right contacts, it is difficult for those hard-working heroes to know where to turn. Local bank managers no longer exist. They need help, guidance and access to funding, preferably local funding, which could buy equity in these would-be expanding businesses. Such local investment funds, allied to training, would be immensely helpful to our nation’s growth, and these local growth funds may even end up being self-funding if the share values go up. I realise that the Government recently produced their SME strategy, which picks up on some of these issues, but I hope that this debate strengthens their resolve to pursue this agenda with a real sense of purpose, knowing that our whole economy and its future growth depend on how successful they are. Above all, we need politicians from all parties to start worrying less about how we spend government money and more about how we can earn it. For some reason this seems a hard ask among politicians, but they should all bear in mind that apart from government borrowing, which must be nearing its limits, every penny spent by government has first to be earned by a business. Every Chancellor before a Budget should have to write that out 100 times: “Every penny spent by government has first to be earned by a business”. We should treat these families running their own businesses as national heroes and value them accordingly. If we are going to kick-start our nation and its economy out of its current doldrums, then these are the people we need. Their efforts should make us proud, but they need all the support we can give them. I look forward to the maiden speech of the noble Lord, Lord McTague, and meanwhile I beg to move.
Lord McTague (Lab) (Maiden Speech)

My Lords, I start with my thanks to the Clerk of the Parliaments, Black Rod, the doorkeepers and the officials for their invaluable support and guidance over the last few weeks. I also thank Members on all sides of the House for their warm welcome. This welcome is especially true of my noble friends Lord Wilson of Sedgefield and Lady Armstrong of Hill Top, and I thank them again. But most of all I thank my wife Sue and my entire family for all their love and support that makes this possible. I think this surreal experience was best summed up by the noble Lord, Lord Cromwell, when he said to me on my entrance to the House: “Welcome to Hogwarts”. Growing up in Birmingham, I never thought this moment was even remotely possible. I did not start life with the proverbial silver spoon. Both my mother and father spent their childhoods in orphanages, but together they created a loving, secure home. Like many baby boomers, I was the first member of my family to go to university. But by the time I was 30 and fed up with the corporate world, I hungered for more purpose and freedom, so in 1987 I started my first business and moved to a village in County Durham. It was there that I met my new MP for the constituency, one Tony Blair. This was the start of the revolution in the Labour Party, and as a small-business owner and a member of that party, I fitted right in. A few years later, I was introduced to a quirky business organisation called the Federation of Small Businesses. Although it had more than 200,000 members, it was struggling to influence government policy. I wanted to change this, so 30 years later I became its national chair, and it is now a brilliant advocate for the nearly 6 million people running small businesses in the UK. It has decided to follow an evidence-led, solution-focused approach which I think a lot of Members of this House will appreciate. All of this means that I feel well-placed to contribute to the substance of today’s debate. It is a debate I feel privileged to be part of and I thank the noble Lord, Lord Cameron of Dillington, for moving it because I share almost all his views on this subject. I passionately believe that small businesses are the key to generating growth in the UK. There is a vast range of businesses that could be defined as family businesses, but they have widely different needs. The biggest issue for large, wealthy family businesses, as has been mentioned on several occasions, is the limit of £2.5 million per estate on the value of assets eligible for 100% property relief. But this is a very small group. Most small businesses will feel no impact from this change. Although I sympathise with the families that run asset-rich but cash-poor businesses, this is not the most important issue affecting small businesses. There are many more issues, several of which were touched on by the noble Lord, Lord Cameron, including business rates, access to finance and, in particular, the regulation of labour. We need to focus on those much bigger issues. But just coming back to the fact that some businesses feel that, in effect, the changes to inheritance tax rule out generation succession, I think we should look at what happens in Germany. They offer special relief for family business succession if the heirs continue to run the business for a continuous period of seven years and maintain payroll levels. Given the healthy state of the German Mittelstand, I think the Minister should look at this as an option for the UK.
The Lord Bishop of Newcastle

My Lords, it is a great pleasure to follow the noble Lord, Lord McTague, and to offer him the warm congratulations of the House and of these Benches on his excellent maiden speech. Although Birmingham has the honour of being his birthplace, the north-east has benefited from his commitment for nearly 40 years. As a fellow northerner, I am delighted to welcome another passionate champion of our region. He remains a long-suffering supporter of Birmingham City. As a follower of Newcastle United, I certainly share some of the footballing challenge in the current landscape. We share a mutual friend in John McCabe, chief executive of the North East Chamber of Commerce, and a conviction that our region has much to contribute to the nation’s future. An engineering graduate of Aston University, the noble Lord brings practical understanding and extensive business experience. Through a decade in senior leadership at the Federation of Small Businesses, including his service as national chair, a role from which he stood down on joining this House, he has championed entrepreneurs across the country. His OBE for services to small businesses recognised that considerable contribution. At a time when growth is firmly on the agenda, he brings wisdom about the people whose enterprise, determination and occasional sleepless nights help to make that possible. His commitment to the north-east extends through his work with the FSB, the CBI and the Legacy Learning Trust in Middlesbrough. He brings valuable experience of the connections between education, opportunity and economic flourishing. I particularly welcome his recognition of the contribution that SMEs can make to tackling the climate crisis. Amid competing demands, that recognition offers a prophetic witness. Caring for our planet belongs at the heart of our economic future. With his wife Sue, four children and nine grandchildren, the noble Lord also has plenty of experience of listening to different views—excellent preparation for your Lordships’ House. We warmly welcome him and look forward to the practical wisdom, insight and concern for the common good that he will bring to our deliberations. I turn now to the debate, and I am grateful to the noble Lord, Lord Cameron, for bringing it to your Lordships’ House. The north-east has always had an entrepreneurial spirit. Greggs began as a family business just around the corner from where I live. Ringtons, Barbour and Fenwick are enduring examples of family ownership—two rooted in Newcastle upon Tyne, the third in South Shields; all founded over a century ago. In Newcastle city centre’s Grainger Market, Robinson’s has served customers since 1929. Britain’s longest established family pet store, it is now run by the th

title: Arts and Cultural Sector:  Employers’ National Insurance
contributions: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (Baroness Mackenzie of Sherwood) (Lab)

I thank the noble Lord for the Question and pay tribute to his unbroken record as the longest-serving Arts Minister. I am sure I will never match it. The 2024 Budget required difficult decisions to fix the public finances. Like other employers, cultural organisations were subject to a 1.2 percentage point increase in employers’ national insurance. To protect the smallest businesses and charities, many of which are cultural or creative organisations, the employment allowance more than doubled from £5,000 to £10,500. This means that 900,000 employers have no employer national insurance liability at all. In addition, earlier this year, we announced a historic £1.5 billion Arts Everywhere package, which is expected to reach 1,000 cultural organisations.
Lord Vaizey of Didcot (Con)

My Lords, I do not wish to make my exchange with the Minister too cosy, but I pay tribute to her and welcome her to her position. She has a distinguished record in the arts, not least from stewarding the Cultural Olympiad during the London Olympics. Nevertheless, I was at a conference yesterday, which was timely, as somebody pointed out that their arts organisation had secured a £50,000 donation that was immediately wiped out by the increase in national insurance contributions. To take one sector—grass-roots music venues—the latest statistics show that one in five people have left that sector because of the impact of national insurance and business rates. This Government seem to give with one hand but take very seriously with the other.
Baroness Mackenzie of Sherwood (Lab)

I thank the noble Lord. As we know, there have been many pressures on cultural and creative organisations. The noble Lord, from his role as a trustee of the Tate, is better placed than I am to comment on the detail of some of those organisations. The impact for many is that they have not yet recovered the audience levels, and therefore incomes, that they enjoyed before Covid. That is probably the biggest threat for many organisations. We are very aware of the many pressures and, as I said, the historic £1.5 billion Arts Everywhere package is a first step in helping to support those organisations.
Baroness Keeley (Lab)

Can my noble friend the Minister tell me her assessment of the damage to the arts and cultural sector if a future Government were to cut the DCMS budget by £1 billion, as was suggested by the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch last week? Take just the music industry: it creates £8 billion a year for the economy and supports 22,000 jobs.
Baroness Mackenzie of Sherwood (Lab)

I thank my noble friend for that question. Like many in the House, I was very shocked by that announcement and that threat against the arts, cultural and creative sectors, which I know many noble Lords in this House support with passion. They contribute to making the creative industries the fastest-growing of the top eight priority business sectors, with a total contribution to the economy of £144 billion last year. I am not going to list their many other benefits on this occasion. I suggest that the best remedy to ensure that the £1 billion cut to the DCMS never happens is to encourage all noble Lords to help Labour win the next election.
Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury (LD)

My Lords, I admire both the noble Lord, Lord Vaizey, and the noble Baroness, Lady Mackenzie, but I add my concern that the party of the noble Lord, Lord Vaizey, has decided to slash all this money for culture and arts. We welcome the Government’s commitment to extra funds for cultural infrastructure, but buildings need people to run them and artists to fill them to draw audiences. However, as we have heard, operating costs have increased significantly and they are struggling. Has the Minister considered something similar to the Irish basic income for artists? Indeed, the Scottish Government have announced plans to pilot an artist’s minimum wage.
Baroness Mackenzie of Sherwood (Lab)

I thank the noble Baroness for that excellent question. The Irish led the way in piloting the idea of an income for artists and there is now a pilot in Scotland. This is something I wish to follow with attention. It is obviously a proposal that is the source of active and enthusiastic lobbying from the arts sector, so I will be paying close attention to how it goes in Scotland.
The Earl of Clancarty (CB)

My Lords, looking further at costs, the Minister will be aware of the now serious crisis in domestic touring of performing arts companies as a result of greatly increased costs, with a catastrophic 64% decline in touring drama since 2019, according to the Arts Council. Will the department impress on the Treasury the importance of expanding tax relief, including theatre tax relief, to make those unavoidable costs of touring fully eligible? Domestic touring is so important for the health of the country.
Baroness Mackenzie of Sherwood (Lab)

As some noble Lords will know, I started my career in touring theatre and worked for many years at a theatre that received touring theatre, so I absolutely understand the issue and its seriousness. It is a subject of lobbying from the sector and of discussion with the Government, and I am unable to comment further on any issue that might or might not appear in the Budget.
Lord Grayling (Con)

My Lords, I declare an interest as a trustee of the National Portrait Gallery. The Minister will be well aware of the importance of philanthropic donations to major institutions. Will she then make representations to the Chancellor to stop government policies that end up with wealthy people who could otherwise support the arts choosing to leave the country?
Baroness Mackenzie of Sherwood (Lab)

I support and publicly pay tribute to all the philanthropists, both those in this country and those based internationally, who support our cultural institutions and arts. It is one of the most important areas of partnership for cultural institutions. A brilliant project that the government art collection announced is the ninth iteration of the Robson-Orr TenTen Awards—an impeccable partnership between philanthropists and the government art collection, co-created and co-inspired by both the philanthropists and the Government. I should pay tribute to the Conservative Government for introducing its ninth iteration, although we celebrate and applaud its achievements to date.
The Lord Bishop of Manchester

My Lords, Britain’s heritage in culture and arts is world-class, but that depends on young people coming forward and having the training, often at a very young age. What more can be done to support the specialist music and dance schools, including Chetham’s School in Manchester, which have been very badly hit by VAT on school fees? That often affects choristers in our cathedrals, and I declare an interest as Bishop of one of those cathedrals. How can we better support those schools so they can survive and thrive and play an important part in bringing forward the next generation of excellent musicians and dancers?
Baroness Mackenzie of Sherwood (Lab)

I thank the right reverend Prelate for the question. I also pay tribute to the brilliant work of Chetham’s, which is an outstanding school. It is unfortunately not possible to exempt a particular sector of private schools from VAT, but for all of us a priority is to ensure that the arts are back in the school curriculum to enable everyone to start along a talent pathway. Not everyone will get into a specialist school like Chetham’s, but everyone should have the opportunity in every postcode to develop their creative talent, and that is a big priority for the Government.
Lord Brennan of Canton (Lab)

My Lords, I want to make two suggestions that the Government might take up to improve matters. One is to extend the sort of tax relief given to film production to our recording studios. A number of us, including the noble Earl, Lord Clancarty, and myself met with the Treasury Ministers earlier this year to discuss that. Will the Minister make representations to the Treasury in that regard? Secondly, something that would cost the Government nothing but that would work is to put the LIVE Trust levy on a statutory footing. Given that, on a voluntary basis, it is collecting less than half the money it could be collecting to support our grass-roots music venues, would she consider legislating in that regard when the Government bring forward their ticketing legislation?
Baroness Mackenzie of Sherwood (Lab)

I thank my noble friend for that. The history in the last 20 years of using tax credits for the benefit of the creative industries is something both sides of the House have greatly pursued, and that has been a very effective way of supporting different sectors within the creative industries. I am aware of the discussions my noble friend refers to. I am unable to comment at the moment on that, but I am happy to explore it further outside this House.

title: Prisons: Foreign National Offenders
contributions: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Ministry of Justice (Lord Lemos) (Lab)

My Lords, within our first two years this Government increased returns of foreign national offenders by 41% compared to the last two years of the previous Government. Between 1 August 2025 and 31 July 2026, more than 3,000 foreign offenders were removed directly from prison under the early removal scheme. Next year, new powers will enable some determinate-sentence foreign national offenders to be deported immediately after sentencing, and we have established a cross-government taskforce to maximise removals.
Baroness Monckton of Dallington Forest (Con)

I thank the noble Lord for his response. However, at a time of chronic prison overcrowding, over 12% of our prison population are foreign national offenders. How many of this cohort who are liable to deportation remain in the United Kingdom due to Article 8 claims and human rights claims? Where this number is not available, why does the Home Office not have this data?
Lord Lemos (Lab)

My Lords, the information that the noble Baroness refers to is held by the Home Office but is not in a reportable format for data extraction purposes. The UK is committed to its human rights obligations at home and abroad, including the European Convention on Human Rights. However, that commitment does not mean complacency. The Chiinău declaration, adopted in May, recognises that the ECHR must not unnecessarily constrain the ability of sovereign states to expel serious criminals, and the Government are also legislating in the Immigration and Asylum Bill currently before the other place.
Baroness Brinton (LD)

My Lords, the Ministry of Justice’s new policy and guidance on foreign nationals in prison, implemented six months ago, is helpfully detailed about what needs to be done to speed up removals. The “Outcomes” section specifically says that there should be: “Increased uptake of voluntary returns … Faster immigration process times … A higher percentage of foreign national prisoners removed under the Early Removal Scheme … Fewer failed removals”, all of which is laudable. However, has the Prison Service been given specific extra resources to achieve those outcomes?
Lord Lemos (Lab)

I thank the noble Baroness for that question. It is an excellent summary of the approach we are taking. HMPPS has a very substantial budget, and we have been working on advancing the deportation of foreign national offenders for many years. The fact is that it has not come down as a proportion. That is why the noble Baroness is right that we need to speed the process up, and that is why we are legislating. We shall of course seek to find the resources to do that.
Lord Garnier (Con)

My Lords, most foreign national prisoners seem to come from Albania, Ireland, Poland, Romania, India and Jamaica. These are all countries with which we have friendly bilateral relations. When did the Minister, or any of his colleagues in his department or in the Home Office or in the Foreign Office, last have a direct conversation with the Governments of those countries better to empty our prisons of overstaying foreign national prisoners?
Lord Lemos (Lab)

Our position on this is that we will use prisoner transfer agreements where they exist and with those countries where we can make such agreements. However, as the noble and learned Lord knows, they are not an easy or quick route. Our commitment is therefore that we will deport foreign national offenders as soon as they have been sentenced. We introduced that in the Sentencing Act and we will commence it in the New Year. We are very serious about this. Of course we will work with our bilateral partners internationally, but it is our commitment that where foreigners commit offences, except for very serious offences, they will be deported.
Viscount Goschen (Con)

The Minister told my noble friend that his department had the data she requested but, unfortunately, it was not in a publishable form. Could he explain that further and perhaps go back to his department, ask it to put that data into publishable form and come back to the House with the numbers that my noble friend requested?
Lord Lemos (Lab)

I am happy to ask the Home Office again; it is not my department, but I speak for the Government. However, my view remains, in relation to putting out data that is misleading or unreliable—I am sorry, but hollow laughter does not help to get to the truth—this is a difficult enough debate in the public square without misleading information.
Lord Keen of Elie (Con)

My Lords, what consideration have His Majesty’s Government given to employing our Brexit freedoms to impose visa controls, sanctions and tariffs against third-party countries that will not accept back the foreign national criminals in our prisons?
Lord Lemos (Lab)

I have already said in response to the noble and learned Lord, Lord Garnier, that our policy is that we intend to deport people who are foreign national offenders. It is not a question of whether countries will accept them. Our intention is to deport them. I have already explained the difficulties with prisoner transfer agreements. By all means we can explore these other routes, but the policy will remain that, if foreign national offenders commit offences in this country then our intention is to deport them, except in the case of very serious offences.
Lord Forbes of Newcastle (Lab)

My Lords, does my noble friend agree that to deport foreign nationals before the end of their sentence served in this country without a cast-iron guarantee that they will serve out the remainder of their sentence in their country of destination would be a travesty of justice for their victims?
Lord Lemos (Lab)

With respect, no, I do not agree with that comment from my noble friend. Of course people who commit offences in this country should be punished, and that is our intention, but, as I have said, we intend to deport people. I do not regard that as a travesty of justice. Being deported from this country and not being allowed to return is a punishment in itself, and that is what we shall do.
Lord Harper (Con)

My Lords, if I may take the Minister back to the original Question and then the follow-up from my noble friend, no one is asking the Government to release inaccurate or misleading data. On the question, the Minister said the Home Office has the data but not in a form capable of being released. The Minister should make sure that it is capable of being released and that it is not misleading, and then make sure that that information is available to both Houses of Parliament and the public. I ask him again: will he go back to the department, make sure that that is done and come back to this House with a commitment and a timetable for producing that important information of enormous public interest?
Lord Lemos (Lab)

We will, of course, discuss with the Home Office and across government how we can make sure, in the interests of transparency and in the interest, if I may say so, of a well-informed public debate, that we get the information out there, but, as I have said, we are not going to put out information that is not in a reportable format. I will go back and ask again, but I doubt that the position is going to change. On the ECHR, I realise now that if you aspire to power in the Tory party then you have to advertise your commitment to getting rid of that convention. That is not this Government’s policy. We are committed to the ECHR.
Baroness Butler-Sloss (CB)
May I ask the Minister what will happen to prisoners who ought to be deported but it is not safe to send them back to their country of origin?
Lord Lemos (Lab)

It is precisely with that in mind that my right honourable friend the Home Secretary is clarifying this in the Immigration and Asylum Bill, so that we can put in place a public interest test to ensure that we can make the right arrangements for these deportations, including respect for their rights under the ECHR.
Lord Watts (Lab)
My Lords, can the Minister explain whether this system of storage of information is new, or whether it was in place for the 14 years that the Tories were in Government?
Lord Lemos (Lab)
It is fair to say that the previous Government did not release this data either.
Lord Bellingham (Con)

My Lords, the Minister has raised the ECHR on a number of occasions, and he himself pointed out some of the constraints that it imposes. He went on to say that it was this Government’s intention to push for reforms of the convention. Can the Minister elaborate on that, and does he really believe in his heart of hearts that our co-partners will allow these changes to take place?
Lord Lemos (Lab)

I am very happy to elaborate on that; I do believe it in my heart of hearts. I also believe in the political declaration from 46 member countries of the Council of Europe which recognised, in the political declaration from the Chiinău meeting—a good word, which I enjoy using from the Dispatch Box—that the ECHR must not unnecessarily constrain the ability of sovereign states to protect their borders or expel serious criminals, and that the threshold for Article 3 in relation to “inhuman or degrading treatment” must remain high and constant. This Government feel that they have done a lot to put that on the agenda of the Council of Europe, and we have received a lot of support for it. So, yes, I do feel optimistic about it.

title: Business of the House
contributions: Jesse Norman (Hereford and South Herefordshire) (Con)
Will the Leader of the House give the House the forthcoming business?
The Leader of the House of Commons (Sir Alan Campbell)

The business for the week commencing 19 October will include: Monday 19 October—Committee of the whole House of the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill, day one. Tuesday 20 October—Conclusion of Committee and remaining stages of the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill. Wednesday 21 October—Consideration of an allocation of time motion, followed by all stages of the Church Appointments (Repeal of Discriminatory Provision) Bill, followed by Opposition day, 4th allotted day, first half, followed by a debate on a motion in the name of the Liberal Democrats, subject to be announced. Thursday 22 October—Tributes to the Clerk of the House, followed by general debate on Black History Month. Friday 23 October—The House will not be sitting. The provisional business for the week commencing 26 October will include: Monday 26 October—General debate on the performance of Royal Mail, followed by general debate on the emerging risks of advanced AI. The subjects for these debates were determined by the Backbench Business Committee. Tuesday 27 October—Second Reading of the Building Safety (Remediation of Unsafe Cladding etc) Bill. Wednesday 28 October—My right hon. Friend the Chancellor of the Exchequer will deliver his Budget statement. Thursday 29 October—Continuation of the Budget debate. Friday 30 October—The House will not be sitting.
Jesse Norman

I thank the Leader of the House for the business. I associate myself with everything that was said in the previous urgent question about the fiasco of the sustainable farming incentive. We meet today on the fifth anniversary of the death—the murder—of Sir David Amess. I know that all colleagues will want to join me in celebrating David, his perennial optimism, his beaming smile, his enormous gift for friendship, and his unfailing energy in assisting and supporting his constituents. The independent report into his murder led by Sir Robert Buckland cannot come too soon. I have three matters to raise. The first relates indirectly to David Amess. As the Leader of the House will know, at Prime Minister’s questions yesterday, the Prime Minister described the man charged with the murder of our former colleague Ann Widdecombe as the man “responsible” for her murder. That statement breached the legal presumption of innocence, discussed a case that is sub judice and misled the House. It must have been inadvertent, but there has been no clarification yet—
Madam Deputy Speaker (Ms Nusrat Ghani)
Order. We do not accuse each other of misleading the House. “Inadvertently” is the word.
Jesse Norman

As I think I said, whatever took place was inadvertent, but there has been no clarification from the Prime Minister or any Minister, no withdrawal of the remark and no apology. That is deeply disrespectful of this House and of the Chair. Will the Leader of the House correct the record, withdraw the remark and apologise on behalf of the Prime Minister? Secondly, as the House will know, Manchester City have been found guilty by an independent commission of 114 of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League, including inaccurate financial reporting, undisclosed remuneration and failure to co-operate with the investigations. This week, having previously been neutral on the issue, the Prime Minister sought to distance himself personally from the club and its owners. Otherwise, he and Ministers have remained remarkably quiet, especially since his club, Everton, had an eight-point deduction for two breaches—112 fewer than have been found here—just three years ago. Will the Leader of the House set out the Government’s position? Do they regard the breaches as extremely serious, or do they believe that a few eggs may have been broken, but broadly speaking everything is all right? When will we get a statement from the Sport Minister on the subject? Finally, last November, I highlighted the severe flooding suffered by Ewyas Harold in my constituency. Homes were inundated, people and businesses were evacuated, and families were left with huge financial and emotional costs. Insurance premiums have gone up—if insurance remains available at all. The school, the doctors’ surgery and access for emergency services were cut off. Other nearby villages, including Clodock, Kentchurch and Allt-yr-ynys were similarly afflicted. Yet now, 11 months later, despite an all-parties meeting that I convened last March and repeated representations to Ministers, the Environment Agency and Herefordshire council, there has been no substantive progress. The Government Office for Science believes El Niño is likely to be bigger than ever this year. My constituents are deeply anxious that floods this winter will drive them yet again from their homes and businesses. Fixing that does not require some vast engineering project. Better drainage, watercourse maintenance, management of run-off and other practical mitigations could all make the difference. However, the residents are in a Catch-22 situation that will be familiar to many people across this House: no one in authority is taking any responsibility, but people are not allowed by law to help themselves. The works could all be done legally, quickly and effectively this year by local companies at less than half the cost of the EA’s framework contractors, but that is prohibited. No one will come to the aid of these people, but put one foot into the watercourse just to clear the debris, and they risk prosecution. I have made a formal Budget submission to the Chancellor on that matter. Will the Leader of the House now take it up personally with the Chancellor and the Environment Secretary and make funding this scheme the first order of business for the Government’s new floods resilience taskforce?
Sir Alan Campbell

May I associate myself absolutely with the comments of the shadow Leader of the House about Sir David Amess? As he said, today is the fifth anniversary of his tragic murder, and I know that the thoughts of the whole House remain with his loved ones. He was well regarded on both sides of the House. He was a mentor to lots of new Members and a fantastic constituency MP. What happened was an absolute tragedy. I welcome Members back to the House after the conference recess, and congratulate my hon. Friend the Member for Holborn and St Pancras (Sagal Abdi-Wali), who joined us on Monday. It is also good to see the shadow Leader of the House in his place. We missed him earlier in the week, and I was concerned that he was still in the half-empty conference hall in Birmingham, wondering whether the shadow Chancellor, the hon. Member for Arundel and South Downs (Andrew Griffith), had actually finished his speech. It was a busy conference season. At the Labour conference, the Prime Minister made several important announcements, including plans for a national care service, which will provide the elderly with free personal care. The Government have also announced that the triple lock will remain until the end of this Parliament, following which it will be adjusted, not least to pay for the new national care service. I do not blame the official Opposition for doing this, because it is part of their job, but they did jump in very quickly to oppose any change to the triple lock. I find that quite surprising, because in August 2021, the shadow Chancellor wrote a comment piece entitled “Unpick the triple lock”, and I understand that the view that it should be unpicked is shared by the current shadow Communities Secretary—the hon. Member for Weald of Kent (Katie Lam)—and at least one former Chancellor. It appears to me that the Conservative party is tying itself in knots on the matter. It would be very helpful if the Leader of the Opposition, or someone from her shadow Cabinet, came to the House to clear up the confusion. Let me turn to the Budget. I did announce, in the forthcoming business, the date of the Budget and the beginning of the debate that will follow. I hope that in that debate the House will be able to reflect on Britain’s economic outlook. To that end, I draw to the House’s attention this week’s positive report from the International Monetary Fund, which upgraded our growth to 1.3% this year, joint second highest in the G7, and the comments of the IMF’s chief economist, who said that the UK “stands out”—his words, not mine—on deficit reduction, with our deficit falling significantly more than other G7 nations’. In other good news this morning, GDP has grown more than expected. We are not complacent, but the Chancellor is absolutely focused on priorities to boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode, all underpinned by the fiscal discipline that characterises this Government. Flood Action Week—this ties in with what the right hon. Gentleman said about the situation in his constituency —started on Monday. The Government have invested £4.2 billion in flood protection measures, and we have new targets to improve flood protection for 200,000 properties. On Monday, we also launched the flood action online portal, which brings together clear, actionable guidance for people to check their flood risk and find the latest weather alerts. On flooding, I thank Members on both sides of the House who have raised the issue regularly at business questions. To address the particular issue that the right hon. Gentleman rightly raised on behalf of his constituents, however, let me say two things further. First, if he wants to make his case to the Floods Minister, I will arrange for him to do so. Secondly, on making representations to the Chancellor, I will ensure that the Chancellor hears what he has said, although I will not say—because I do not know—what is in the Budget. On the other points the right hon. Member made, I am not sure that he is being characteristically fair, as he normally is, because the Prime Minister has acknowledged that he misspoke. The right hon. Gentleman was out quite quickly, and rightly, to make his case yesterday, and the Prime Minister did respond. He said that he misspoke, he has apologised and he has corrected the record. There is no excuse for misspeaking in the House and I am not trying to explain that away, but this Prime Minister is characterised by an authenticity and a passion in the way that he responds. It is not unusual for Prime Ministers or anybody else to misspeak in the House. As long as they correct the record, which he has done, that should be put into perspective. The right hon. Gentleman also raises the issue of Manchester City, and the Prime Minister again has been characteristically clear. He has made it clear that the initial judgment on the club is very serious and that no one is suggesting that anybody is above the rules. There is an ongoing independent process. It is important that it is allowed to run its course as quickly and as fairly as possible. At the end of that, if the Sport Minister needs to come to make a statement to this House, I am quite sure that she will do so.
David Burton-Sampson (Southend West and Leigh) (Lab)

As the shadow Leader of the House and the Leader of the House have pointed out, today is the fifth anniversary of the tragic murder of Sir David Amess in my constituency. My thoughts are with his family, his Conservative colleagues here and in Southend and all colleagues and constituents who knew Sir David. As his plaque behind me says, may his light remain. The Children’s Parliament was founded by Sir David Amess, and it was a project that was close to his heart. I am delighted that, on this anniversary, we will be joined by the child MPs in Parliament, and I am sure that it will be a lively debate. Will the Leader of the House join me in celebrating the enthusiasm of these children, who are showing a keen interest in democracy at a young age?
Sir Alan Campbell

I certainly join my hon. Friend in everything he said about Sir David Amess and in recognising the importance that he gave to involving young people in our parliamentary process. To that end, I welcome the child MPs to the House today. I wish them well in everything they do, and it is important that we support not just their learning about the political process but exploring how they can contribute more to it.
Madam Deputy Speaker (Ms Nusrat Ghani)
I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.
Bobby Dean (Carshalton and Wallington) (LD)

I join the Leader of the House in this tribute to Sir David Amess. It is clear how well loved he was across the House, and our thoughts are with his family. The Leader of the House mentioned the party conference season. The Liberal Democrats warmly welcome the Prime Minister moving towards our positions on Europe, social care and electoral reform at conference. We urge him to go further and faster on all three fronts. [ Interruption. ] Not appreciated by those on the Conservative Benches, but we certainly appreciate progress on Europe, social care and electoral reform. There is an emerging scandal that relates to the treatment of Hongkongers entitled to British national overseas status. The UK has a historic commitment to those people, with the promise of democracy being maintained in Hong Kong or a pathway to UK citizenship, which many of them have taken up. However, we have received reports that many BNO applications are now being refused on the basis of past convictions in Hong Kong. UK rules state that if the conviction is an offence in the UK and the sentence is for longer than 12 months, that should result in an automatic refusal. Some Hongkongers were convicted for longer than 12 months for the offence of rioting, which is an offence in the UK but, of course, they were not really rioting; they were engaging in peaceful democratic protest. We have raised these concerns directly with the Home Office, which says that discretion can be applied, but the guidance we have seen says otherwise. The fact is that people are now being rejected on this basis. To add insult to injury, the rejection letters say that these decisions have been made by a competent foreign court. I hope the Leader of House will agree that this would be a betrayal of the UK’s historic commitment to those people, so can he organise for Ministers to issue clear guidance about the specific discretion that is required in these cases?
Sir Alan Campbell

I am sure the House will not have missed the hon. Gentleman’s opening comments when he talked about his party’s “positions” on Europe—it is not unusual for the Lib Dems to have many positions on many things. I am sure he enjoyed his conference, not least because he probably got more sleep than he might have done with a young child at home, but there we are. The difference between our conference and his is that the leader of our party came out strengthened from our conference; I am not sure the Lib Dems can say the same. On the serious matter that the hon. Gentleman raises, we have granted over 230,000 visas under the British national overseas visa route, and we are honouring our commitment to support Hongkongers facing political pressure. We remain committed to supporting Hong Kong residents and welcoming eligible applications under the scheme. Every application involving a prior conviction is assessed individually on its merits. We are ensuring that actions that are not considered criminal offences under UK law do not bar applicants from safety, but I give him my word that I will go back to the Home Office, and if that needs to be clarified, I will draw that to its attention
Torcuil Crichton (Na h-Eileanan an Iar) (Lab)

The Western Isles have been struck this week by maritime tragedy with the sinking of the fishing vessel Kilda in a Tuesday night storm off the coast of Lewis, with what we fear is the subsequent loss of the three souls aboard. I pay tribute and express thanks to the coastguard officers, the Royal National Lifeboat Institution crews, helicopter crews and police officers who are still involved in the search for two of the missing men. Events like this cut deeply into our communities and leave salted wounds of grief; I think of Ness, Barvas and Carloway, and the homes and villages there that this crew left from. That pain of grief will be echoed in other coastal communities across the country. All those who fish will mourn, and they that spread their nets on the ocean will languish. For that reason, can the Leader of the House join me in expressing deep condolences to the families and communities affected and to all the other families and fishers who touch that razor’s edge of the deep every day and, for our good, go down to the sea in ships?
Sir Alan Campbell

I am sure the whole House will join me and the hon. Gentleman in extending our most heartfelt condolences to the friends and families of those who have lost their lives. I join him in paying tribute to the brave members of the RNLI and the coastguard involved in the search and rescue. I am a coastal MP, and it is coming up to the 60th anniversary of the loss of the Gaul, the biggest single trawler loss in the industry’s history; six of those men were from my constituency, and we marked that event over the summer. I know absolutely the importance of that loss and how it is felt in fishing communities, and I know how important the work of the RNLI and coastguard is and how deeply appreciated they are.
Madam Deputy Speaker (Ms Nusrat Ghani)
I call the Chair of the Backbench Business Committee.
Bob Blackman (Harrow East) (Con)

I join others in paying tribute to the late Sir David Amess. He was always here for business questions, with a topical question and a smile on his face. I thank the Leader of the House for announcing the business on 26 October in the Chamber. Given the experience on Monday, I thank him for giving protected time for the baby loss awareness debate. Considering how many times the issue was raised at Business, Innovation, Science and Trade questions this morning, the debate on the performance of Royal Mail is likely to be extremely well attended. Will the Leader of the House consider giving protected time for those two debates, particularly if there will be Government statements or urgent questions? The business in Westminster Hall for next week is as follows. On 20 October, there will be a debate on manufacturing skills. On Thursday 22 October, there will be a statement from the Science and Technology Committee, followed by a debate on compensation for Equitable Life policyholders, followed by a debate on the legacy of the Jarrow crusade on its 90th anniversary. On 27 October there will be a debate on recognising the production and serving of cask ale as an intangible cultural heritage. Personally, I prefer drinking it to talking about it. On Thursday 29 October there will be a debate on the mandatory safeguarding 24/7 of helipads at major trauma centres, followed by a debate on the role and effectiveness of Ofcom. I have a couple of housekeeping notes. We are short of a Labour Member on the Backbench Business Committee; I hope that space will be filled quickly. This week we had a problem, because we had the bare quorum needed to do our business. We had an application for a debate on Black History Month, but I note that is now a Government debate. The risk is that the Front Benchers will get two bites at the cherry, which reduces the time for Back Benchers to contribute. This would have been a Backbench Business Committee debate, led by Back Benchers, but I completely understand the Leader of the House wishing to offer a general debate on the subject. We are halfway through Navaratri, a celebration for Hindus across the world. It is a joyous occasion. Last Saturday, I attended the World Sindhi Congress, and this week I received a delegation of ex-Bangladeshi politicians and Sanatans. They raised the same issue: the plight of Hindus in Pakistan and Bangladesh is desperate right now. I receive messages literally every day about atrocities committed against the Hindu population of Bangladesh and Pakistan.
