I know that the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office is concentrating on the illegal war between Russia and Ukraine, and the crisis in the middle east, but could we have a statement on what the Government will do to help protect those minorities in Pakistan and Bangladesh?
Sir Alan Campbell

As ever, I thank the hon. Gentleman for his work chairing the Committee, and indeed I thank the whole Committee for its work. On the baby loss debate, not only was the allocated time protected, but there was an element of discipline, which I welcome. I do not think the approach is perfect, but we are getting there. I will bear in mind what he says about Monday 26 October. My initial reaction is that it is not always necessary or welcome to have guaranteed time for debates, and perhaps we should take this on a case-by-case basis, but I will give some thought to what he says. I take away the point about ensuring that the Committee has full membership, and I will seek to ensure that the issue is resolved as quickly as possible. I will also ask the Front-Bench spokespersons for Black History Month to bear in mind what he said, and to ensure that in the debate on the subject, Back Benchers—it would probably otherwise have been a Backbench Business debate—get the time that they need. I will get to the hon. Gentleman’s serious point about the protection of minorities, but it would be remiss of me not to send our most heartfelt condolences to the friends and family of those impacted by the tragic school collapse in Pakistan; news of it came out overnight. I hope the whole House will join me in sending our heartfelt best wishes to those communities. On the treatment of Hindus and others, the UK strongly condemns all instances of hate or violence directed towards minority religious communities in Pakistan, including Shi’a Muslims, Ahmadis, Christians, Hindus and Sikhs. We work with the international community to promote human rights, in partnership with Pakistan, but I will draw the hon. Gentleman’s comments to the attention of the FCDO. I hear what he says about there being lots of other things going on, not least what is happening in Ukraine and the middle east, but that is no excuse for our taking our eye off the ball in situations where we can do something to help.
Tulip Siddiq (Hampstead and Highgate) (Lab)

Vincent Chan abused baby girls at a Bright Horizons nursery in my constituency for seven years. The Guardian has now revealed that three years before he was arrested, a complaint was made about him. It was investigated by Bright Horizons, overseen by Camden council, who cleared him and allowed him to return to work, where he continued to abuse little children until he was arrested. I have asked Camden council and Bright Horizons for the full documentation relating to the investigation that took place in 2021. Can we have a debate in Government time about strengthening the safeguarding practices in nurseries, particularly in the Bright Horizons chain? Ofsted has taken the unprecedented step of issuing two welfare requirement notices to the nurseries in that chain.
Sir Alan Campbell

I thank my hon. Friend for raising this matter again. She is doing an excellent job of keeping it at the forefront of our mind. The safeguarding of young children is our utmost priority. Over the summer, we have announced a range of measures to improve early years safeguarding. The Department for Education has established an expert advisory group on safeguarding, which is looking at the use of CCTV and digital devices in early years settings; it will report before Christmas. If she is seeking a meeting with the Department to get an update on these matters, I will help her to arrange one.
Martin Vickers (Brigg and Immingham) (Con)

Like many Members from across the House who attended their party conference, I visited the Guide Dogs stand at our party conference. The organisation made the point, as it regularly does, about the dangers of pavement parking, not only to those with guide dogs, but to the disabled and other groups. The Government recently had a consultation on the subject, and have taken the view that further legislation is needed. Devolving the power to local authorities is fine, but they need to have resources available to them. Will the Leader of the House arrange for a statement from the appropriate Minister?
Sir Alan Campbell

I too met Guide Dogs at our conference. It does a fantastic job campaigning on a really important issue. As the hon. Gentleman said, the Government have taken some steps forward on this issue, but we recognise that there are more things to do. I cannot guarantee him a statement on the subject, but if he wants to hear from the mouths of Ministers about our plans, he might seek a Westminster Hall debate or Adjournment debate on the issue.
Kim Johnson (Liverpool Riverside) (Lab)

Palestinian families have been denied family reunification, and that has been found to be unlawful in the courts. Those families include those of Obaida and Mahmoud, two boys who, last year, met the former Prime Minister, who promised to do everything that he could to ensure that their families were united with them. Will the Leader of the House allow a debate in Government time on a Palestinian visa scheme, so that we can scrutinise these important issues?
Sir Alan Campbell

My hon. Friend is a strong advocate on these issues. If she seeks an Adjournment debate or a Westminster Hall debate on the subject, she could put these matters directly to Ministers. The Government are keen to do all we can on this, but an Adjournment debate or a Westminster Hall debate is the way forward for her.
Madam Deputy Speaker (Ms Nusrat Ghani)
I call the Father of the House.
Sir Edward Leigh (Gainsborough) (Con)

On the Church Appointments (Repeal of Discriminatory Provision) Bill, I am not sure that many of us Jews and Catholics have really felt discriminated against since 1829 by the provisions that are being repealed, and we think that there may be more important things for the Government to do. I am not sure that many of us actually want to be involved in appointing Anglican bishops, although we might improve the number of bishops who talk about God, rather than social issues. Turning to the much more immediate and important issue of the restoration and renewal of Parliament, the Leader of the House knows that I have been involved in this subject for many years, and am constantly urging action. We really need to get on with it. We need to repeal the legislation that stops work carrying on around us. There is a horrible rumour that we are going back to delaying the whole thing until 2032, and there is talk about a full decant. Will he give us a report on how we will get on with repairing this building?
Sir Alan Campbell

I am sure that the right hon. Gentleman will make his points about the Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829, and the discrimination against Jews under the provisions from the 1860s, which banned them from doing certain things, in the debate, if he is able to. The difference is that we have a Catholic Prime Minister, so it is key that nothing gets in the way of him taking part in any deliberations. I am sure that the House is keen to make these changes to outdated legislation. There is a report suggesting a way forward on restoration and renewal. I have committed to bringing forward a motion on the subject, because I absolutely agree with the right hon. Gentleman: it is time that we got on with this work. There is not full agreement across the House about what that means, but it is important that we get a debate. He should not believe everything that he is told, or reads, about any postponement. The purpose is not to postpone restoration and renewal; the reality is that it has been postponed for far too long. The longer we postpone it, the more it costs not just to keep this place functioning, but to eventually get round to doing something about it. However, I admit that my approach has not been to rush into this work, or to get the House to rush into it, because I want consensus, if we can get it. That is the best way of going forward. There is not a consensus, but we can work toward one. I want to build in as many safeguards as possible. For example, I would like to see the outcome of the inquiry by the Public Accounts Committee. Quite rightly, MPs will ask, “How do you ensure that this work will provide value for money, if you decide to do it?”. On timing, all I would say is that we need to get on with this work, so watch this space.
Marsha De Cordova (Battersea) (Lab)

The Albert bridge in Battersea has been closed for more than eight months, amid safety concerns. That is causing severe delays and disruption to my constituents and businesses alike. Bridges in Battersea and across London play a vital role in keeping London moving, so can we have a debate in Government time on how we can make our bridges a strategic asset under national Government oversight?
Sir Alan Campbell

My hon. Friend may want to make that point directly either to Ministers in the Department for Transport or, if we are talking about essential infrastructure, to the Cabinet Office. I can help arrange that for her. She could also seek a debate on the subject, because I am sure that there are colleagues across the House, not least from London, who will share her frustration about what is happening. They could then hear from a Minister on how the Government could best resolve the matter.
Mike Martin (Tunbridge Wells) (LD)

I do not know if the Leader of the House has seen “The Wargame”, a recent series on Sky, but its central message is that we are not ready. We might be more ready, had the promised defence readiness Bill come into this Session of Parliament, but it was inexplicably dropped from His Majesty’s Speech. Are there plans to bring that Bill forward at some point? Has he had, or will he have, any conversations with the Defence Secretary to hasten it along?
Sir Alan Campbell

This Session is quite crowded, and one should not read into the fact that a Bill does not appear in it that it is not important to the Government. It is sometimes a question of priority, and what needs to be done. I hear what the hon. Gentleman says, but the Government are absolutely committed to doing everything we can to ensure that we in this country stand by our allies and are able to defend ourselves. I will not speculate about what is in the third Session of this Parliament, but I will give this some thought, and will talk to the Defence Secretary, as the hon. Gentleman suggests, to ensure that this is at the forefront of his mind.
David Pinto-Duschinsky (Hendon) (Lab)

Sometimes in our lives, we are fortunate to meet someone truly inspirational. Rabbi Bernd Koschland was such a person. Bernd came to this country in the Kindertransport, aged just eight. His parents were not so lucky; he never saw them again. Many of us would have been broken by such a tragedy, but Bernd triumphed over that adversity. He dedicated his life to education, teaching generation after generation and telling his story to children around the globe. In 2018, he was awarded an MBE for his role as one of this country’s leading Holocaust educators. Bernd was a man of huge compassion, warmth, humility and humour. He loved his family and was a proud great-grandfather. It was my honour to call him a friend, and to talk to him almost every week for many years. We lost Bernd over the recess. Our community in Hendon mourns him deeply, but his legacy will live on. Will the Leader of the House join me in celebrating Bernd’s life, thanking him for his huge contribution to this country and passing on this House’s deepest condolences to his family?
Sir Alan Campbell

Yes, I will. Rabbi Bernd Koschland led a remarkable life. He dedicated himself to educating us about the horrors of the Holocaust, which we must never, ever forget, and we are eternally grateful to him for his significant contribution to our country. I am sure that the whole House will join me in sending our condolences to his friends, family and all those who knew him.
Madam Deputy Speaker (Ms Nusrat Ghani)
I call Sir Julian Lewis—it is nice to see you so calm today.
Sir Julian Lewis (New Forest East) (Con)

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker. May I invite the Leader of the House and other colleagues to do their best to watch the 15-minute video on the Maze YouTube channel entitled “The Medical Mesh Scandal Ruining Women’s Lives”, which was screened last night at a meeting chaired excellently by the hon. Member for Washington and Gateshead South (Mrs Hodgson)? That video deals, of course, with the scandal of pelvic mesh. title: Sovereign Grant Bill
contributions: The Parliamentary Secretary, HM Treasury (Lord Pitt-Watson) (Lab)

My Lords, this Bill relates to the sovereign grant, which Parliament has provided to support the official duties of the monarch and the work of the Royal Household. The Bill implements the conclusions of a recent royal trustees’ review of the sovereign grant. It does three things. First, it will reset the grant level for the next financial year at £99.9 million, with the anticipation that this will be the grant for the next five years. Currently, the grant is £137.9 million. This gives effect to the commitment of successive Governments, and the expectation of the Royal Household, to a reduction in the level of funding following the completion of the Buckingham Palace reservicing programme. The Bill also aims to make two targeted improvements to the statutory framework for this funding, introducing limited flexibilities to ensure that funding levels remain appropriate, both on an annual basis and within each year, in response to exceptional circumstances. This will make it easier to respond where funding would become inappropriately low or high. The sovereign grant supports the monarch’s official duties; it funds the staff, official travel, property maintenance and essential services required for the sovereign to fulfil their unique constitutional role. That role extends beyond ceremonial functions: it includes hosting Heads of State, supporting diplomatic engagement, representing the United Kingdom overseas and strengthening our relationships across the Commonwealth and the world. These activities support UK interests, including trade, investment, security and diplomacy. At home, the grant supports the sovereign’s significant role, from recognising charitable and voluntary service to bringing communities together across the United Kingdom. I note that, with a new and younger monarch, there have been more activities than in the immediate past. I turn to the Bill. Since 2012, the level of the sovereign grant has been determined through a statutory framework established by Parliament in the Sovereign Grant Act 2011. That framework requires the annual grant amount to be calculated by reference to the previous year’s expenditure and a percentage of the profits of the Crown Estate, which is an independent corporation, the net revenue profits of which are returned to the Exchequer. To ensure that the funding levels remain appropriate, the 2011 Act also requires that the royal trustees—the Prime Minister, the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the Keeper of the Privy Purse—conduct regular reviews. A key piece of context for the House is that Parliament agreed a temporary uplift in the grant from 2017-18 to 2026-27 to fund the Buckingham Palace reservicing programme. That programme has been a major 10-year investment to modernise ageing infrastructure, replace critical electrical and mechanical systems and safeguard the long-term future of one of the nation’s most important historic buildings. As that programme nears completion, now is the time for the level of funding to be reassessed. Earlier this year, the then royal trustees completed the latest review and considered the Royal Household’s projected expenditure and the Crown Estate’s projected revenues for the period of 2027-32. The trustees concluded that, with the Buckingham Palace reservicing programme nearing completion, the exceptional funding requirement that justified the temporary uplift no longer existed. They therefore recommended that the level of the sovereign grant should fall from £137.9 million in 2026-27 to £99.9 million in 2027-28. That represents a reduction of almost £38 million, or more than a quarter, compared to the current year. At the same time, the trustees recognised that the Royal Household continues to face operational pressures. For example, the recommended level of funding will enable the household to address a maintenance backlog that was exacerbated by the pandemic and replace ageing digital infrastructure to strengthen cyber security. The grant level provided for by the Bill therefore ensures value for money for taxpayers and that the Royal Household can continue to discharge its functions effectively. In conclusion, the Bill delivers a fair and proportionate funding settlement. It will reduce the level of the sovereign grant following the completion of the major capital programme, improve the resilience and sustainability of the statutory framework while maintaining parliamentary oversight, and ensure that the sovereign grant can continue to fulfil its core purpose: supporting the official duties of the monarch and maintaining the occupied palaces on behalf of the nation. I beg to move.
Lord Redwood (Con)

My Lords, I support the Minister in his aims and am pleased that he set out so well the important work that the Royal Family does on behalf of our country, promoting our diplomatic efforts, entertaining important guests of the nation and supporting the Government of the day in the work that they are doing in trade, diplomacy and wider world affairs. I accept fully the Minister’s case that this needed review. I was a supporter of extra money being made available to renovate and modernise Buckingham Palace—it is a most important national building and, importantly, a working building. So many people have the pleasure of going there and so many of our international guests have the privilege of a great dinner or social event at the palace, which they normally much value because it is something that many other countries in the world cannot match. I broadly welcome this legislation and agree that the amount should be adjusted downwards, but I would like to stress that the amount must be sufficient and the formula and details for future years sufficiently well thought through that we accommodate without argument or unseemly exchanges the legitimate increases in costs that will clearly take place, as inflation still stalks our land and as modernisation and the amount of service we expect will probably increase. We should expect the amount of money to go up. I am sure my noble friend on the Front Bench will rightly have detailed issues to raise, but I think it will be in the spirit that we fully support the monarchy in its work and believe that there should be a proper sovereign grant. I leave one last thought with the Minister that he may be able to clarify at the end. It is good to have a formula that you can normally rely on and that gives a fairly predictable outcome, as it allows the Royal Household to plan rather than having to battle over budgets year by year in the way that others may have to do, because that is a distraction and, if it gets into the press, would be damaging to the very diplomatic image we are trying to create.
Lord Foulkes of Cumnock (Lab Co-op)

My Lords, I have great respect for the Minister. As a fellow Scot, he will make sure that every bawbee gets value for money. I understand that he will have had a brief from down the Corridor. In fact, having read Commons Hansard , the words were quite familiar. But I hope that he will listen to the debate here in the House of Lords and transmit the views of Members, because unfortunately the Bill was not given the full scrutiny it deserved on the Floor of the House of Commons, which was rather regrettable. The Lords needs to give it some scrutiny today. Although we are not in a position to table any amendments because, understandably, the Speaker of the House of Commons has designated this as a money Bill, we still have a duty to shine a light on the inequality built into this mechanism and the lack of transparency and accountability. The reality is simple. If the Government genuinely wanted a needs-based system, the Royal Household would submit an annual Budget request to the Treasury like any other public entity. Instead, we now have a formula tied to Crown Estate profits. That is a system designed as a “heads I win, tails you lose” proposition—frozen against losses when profits fall, yet fully open to the upside when they surge. When we ask the public to fund an institution to the tune of about £100 million a year through the sovereign grant, at a time when, sadly, we know many people in this country face severe pressure on their household budgets, we here have a duty to ask two fundamental questions: first, are we getting value for money and, secondly, do the actions of the institution match the value that it preaches? I argue that in both cases the answer is no. We hear various royal pronouncements on climate change, yet official reports reveal hundreds of private jet and helicopter flights for short domestic trips, one recently to the races where the royal concerned could have easily gone by car. The taxpayer has funded two new helicopters for the Royal Family, whereas Mountain Rescue has to raise money for its helicopters through charitable efforts. Is that right in the 21st century? Then we see commendable statements on homelessness, from the Prince of Wales in particular, but the Crown maintains many empty or underutilised luxury estates across the country: in Scotland at Balmoral, in London—not just Buckingham Palace but all over the city—and at Sandringham. In terms of value for money, our monarchy remains by a vast margin the most expensive state-funded royal family in Europe. In Spain, the public grant is only about £7 million. In Sweden, it is under £15 million, and in the Netherlands, it is £45 million. In European terms, we are one of the big spenders, as far as the Royal Family is concerned. If we take a baseline of 2011, £31 million, and adjust that for inflation, our sovereign grant, even allowing for this kind of expenditure, would be between £45 million and £50 million, not the £99.9 million proposed. That figure does not even account for police security; I have had letters from local councils about the cost that they are required to meet for security. The tax advantages of the income from the Duchies are not taken account of. I am not challenging the role of the sovereign, in particular, but while European neighbours have streamlined their royal houses, we continue to fund a sprawling network of so-called working royals on ribbon-cutting duties or pulling open tableaux. That is not real work. It is not like a teacher who works five days a week or a nurse in a geriatric hospital who might be working a 12-hour shift. It is not real work that they do. I might just say that Princess Anne is a notable exception. It is interesting that all her offspring have given up their royal titles and work for a living. Perhaps that is an example that other members of the Royal Family might think about. The fundamental issue here is accountability. When George Osborne introduced the sovereign grant, he claimed that removing parliamentary debate would depoliticise the monarchy. In reality, it has stripped away democratic oversight, and the tightening of freedom of information rules means that transparency is now virtually impossible, breaking the assurances that were given previously to Parliament. Shielding the institution behind FoI exemptions and blocking debate has enabled a runaway increase in public funding. To achieve such accountability, three key actions are necessary, and I sincerely ask the Minister to take account of the debate here today and to take these suggestions to his fellow Ministers in the Treasury and elsewhere. We should consider, first, a return to annual parliamentary scrutiny through regular debates and votes, as with other public bodies. Secondly, we should also treat the Royal Household like any other public body under the Freedom of Information Act. Thirdly, we should ask the Commons to task its Public Accounts Committee to conduct a full, root-and-branch review of all royal funding and finances. Parliament is here to safeguard public money, and it is time we modernised, streamlined and properly brought transparency to this institution. I hope the Minister will genuinely and sincerely take account of this debate and, with colleagues, look again at this matter.
Lord Sikka (Lab)

My Lords, it is a great pleasure to follow my noble friend Lord Foulkes of Cumnock. This Bill comes at a time when many households are struggling to make ends meet. Under this Bill, the core funding of the Royal Household—that is, after ignoring the money allocated for refurbishment of Buckingham Palace—rises from £51.8 million for 2024-25 to £99.9 million for 2027-28. That is an increase of 97%. I am not aware of any ordinary household that has secured an increase of this magnitude in its income to discharge its essential duties. The average real wage of workers has barely changed since 2008; 25.3 million people live below the minimum income standard. Around 300,000 people a year are dying while waiting for an NHS hospital appointment, but here we are giving away a large chunk of money. This massive increase is being given to a family which, according to Forbes magazine, could be worth £21 billion. Anyone with lifetime savings of over £16,000 is generally disqualified or severely restri

title: US-Russia Deal on Diesel Exports:  Effect on Ukraine
contributions: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (Lord Wood of Anfield) (Lab)

My Lords, the quickest way to get diesel back on to world markets is a full energy ceasefire, with both sides, Ukraine and Russia, stopping attacks. We therefore welcome President Trump’s call for a reciprocal energy ceasefire and President Zelensky’s readiness to implement it once a start date is confirmed. The Prime Minister reiterated his complete solidarity with Ukraine and our determination to strengthen sanctions on Russia when he spoke to President Zelensky on Saturday, ahead of further talks in London today.
Lord McConnell of Glenscorrodale (Lab)

I thank my noble friend the Minister and the Prime Minister for their strong words of solidarity with President Zelensky and the people of Ukraine. I am sure that Members across your Lordships’ House will today welcome President Zelensky to London and express full solidarity with him in this very difficult week for him and his people. The coalition of the willing was established to provide diplomatic and material support for the Ukrainian Government and the people of Ukraine in this constant fight for their sovereignty. The coalition includes most European countries, but also, of course, Japan, Australia, New Zealand and Canada. What are the Government doing to look at expanding the coalition, in these challenging circumstances, to involve more countries in providing that material and diplomatic support, and what is being done to mobilise the coalition to support Ukraine through what is going to be a very difficult winter ahead?
Lord Wood of Anfield (Lab)

I thank my noble friend for that question and reiterate what he said about how welcome President Zelensky is today. I had the privilege, in fact, of greeting him on his arrival in central London and he will be having discussions with the Prime Minister later on. My noble friend is also right that the coalition of the willing serves a number of functions. It serves the primary function, as my noble friend said, of providing military support. I am pleased to say that under both Conservative and Labour Governments, in the last four and a half years, we have provided more than £25 billion of support. The coalition also provides budgetary support for Ukraine’s finances, which have been catastrophically affected by the conflict. It provides constant diplomatic support, but it also thinks ahead to a world in which security guarantees will be needed and looks to think about arrangements for that. As for expanding the coalition of the willing, my noble friend is right. There is scarcely a meeting that I or the Foreign Secretary have in which we do not talk about the help that existing and prospective members of the coalition can provide, and that will continue to be a theme of our discussions.
Lord Bruce of Bennachie (LD)

This deal is outrageous and unnecessary, because the President is lifting sanctions on Russia and threatening new sanctions on Ukraine. No wonder the United States Senate Committee on Foreign Relations said that the United States “should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians”. Will the British Government, when meeting President Zelensky in London today, not only repeat that we stand four-square behind Ukraine but say that we are angered and dismayed that the White House is acting for Putin?
Lord Wood of Anfield (Lab)

I thank the noble Lord for that question. We will certainly be reiterating, and have reiterated already, our unquestioning and continuing support for Ukraine—military, budgetary, diplomatic and other kinds of support. As my right honourable friend the Defence Secretary said on Sunday, we have made different choices. We think—I am pleased to say that this is across the coalition of the willing more broadly —that the approach to Russia has to be consistently focused on exerting pressure through sanctions and other kinds of pressure to force Russia to the table that President Zelensky has already said he is prepared to go to, to discuss a ceasefire and future arrangements.
Lord Harper (Con)

The Minister is right in saying that there is cross-party support for supporting Ukraine and President Zelensky, and I am happy to reiterate mine for that. However, there are still European countries, I understand, that are purchasing gas from Russia. Do the Government have any plans at the summit that they are having with the European Union in November to raise this issue and take steps to persuade those countries that purchasing gas from Russia is helping to fund its military campaign against Ukraine?
Lord Wood of Anfield (Lab)

I thank the noble Lord for that question. He puts his finger on an extremely important point. Again, in my short time so far at the Foreign Office, I have seen an extreme amount of attention focused on continuing economic relationships, not just in Europe but in central Asia and elsewhere. It is something that the Foreign Office and the Government more broadly take very seriously. We have a variety of tools we try to use to put pressure on and encourage countries to reduce their economic relationship with Russia. The EU-UK summit in late November is primarily about the UK’s relationship with the European Union in the light of the Brexit treaty and arrangements for that, but I can assure the noble Lord that the issue he raises is at the forefront of desks across the Foreign Office in our relationships with multiple countries.
Lord Cromwell (CB)

My Lords, does the Minister agree with me that the President of the United States—a country which prizes and fought for its own independence—could indeed leave a genuine, positive legacy as a peacemaker if, instead of doing business deals with Russia’s current regime, he sought a peace in Ukraine that does not involve simply handing over that country to a terrorist state bent on colonising its neighbours? A one-word answer will suffice.
Lord Wood of Anfield (Lab)

Okay. It is inconceivable, in my view, that peace, which we all desperately want in this conflict, will occur without the full engagement of the United States. Encouraging the United States to play that positive role and to continue many of the positive contributions it has made to securing that peace is an important thing for all parties in this conflict.
Lord Callanan (Con)

My Lords, across this House we have maintained an important consensus on the need for us all to stand fully behind Ukraine. I agree with the Minister, and indeed the Prime Minister, on the need for further sanctions against Russia. However, on 26 March, Keir Starmer announced that he had given approval for Russia’s shadow fleet tankers to be seized if they transited through UK waters, and this was widely welcomed. Since then, we have intercepted a grand total of one from the dozens which have transited through the English Channel. Can we expect some more robust action from this new Government in halting these uninsured and dangerous vessels?
Lord Wood of Anfield (Lab)

I thank the noble Lord for that question. He is right to point to the importance of disrupting the shadow fleet, but I am pleased to say that the UK is playing a leading role in doing precisely that. By some estimates, Putin has spent more than $14 billion in establishing the shadow fleet. We have now specified more than 640 vessels under the Russia sanctions regime, including more than 600 oil tankers and 20 liquefied natural gas carriers. There is much more to be done; there is more that will be done; and there is more that will be done to encourage other nations to have the courage to do what we did. This is at the centre of the leading thinking about effective responses to Russia, and the UK is proud to be in the vanguard of that.
Lord Touhig (Lab)

My Lords, I serve on the Council of Europe parliamentary network on the situation of children in Ukraine. The Russians have deported 20,651 children from occupied Ukraine to Russia. The children are told that they are now Russians. They are made to learn Russian and are being offered up for adoption by Russian families. Older teenagers are put into training camps in preparation for taking part in military action against Ukraine. Therefore, I ask my noble friend for help. Will the Government remind our American friends of this before they make any deals like the one we are talking about today?
Lord Wood of Anfield (Lab)

I am very glad my noble friend has raised this issue. I was in Ukraine three weeks ago and visited an organisation that focuses on tracing stolen children and trying to bring about the judicial proceedings to bring them back. The number is actually probably greater than 20,000. It is heartbreaking to hear these stories, and it is extraordinary work that these organisations and the Office of the President of Ukraine are doing. I was in Toronto last week at an international conference precisely on the issues of detained Ukrainian civilians and stolen children—because that is what they are: children who have been stolen from their families and forced into adoption throughout Russia. Some 60 to 70 countries signed pledges and committed to further budgetary and other kinds of support, and we are going to continue to encourage all nations to put this at the forefront of their thinking about the Ukraine conflict.
Lord Purvis of Tweed (LD)

My Lords, the Government put forward an open-ended exemption on their sanctions against refined oil products from Russia; this could potentially now include products imported via the United States under this deal with America. Under pressure from these Benches, Minister Stephen Doughty wrote to me on 11 June, saying that there was now a sunset clause on that extension set for 1 January, and we welcome that. Can the Minister be absolutely clear to the House that, even if there is pressure from Trump’s Administration, that sunset clause will not be altered, and we will ensure that there is a full and comprehensive ban on Russian refined oil products in the UK?
Lord Wood of Anfield (Lab)

I thank the noble Lord for the question. He has focused on this before and he is right to focus on it. Obviously, I am not going to discuss the details of individual sanctions. Sanctions policy is a crucial but extremely complex area. It is complex partly because of re-importation and relabelling, and partly because sanctions measures incentivise countries to get around those measures through further arrangements, so our sanctions policy has to remain vigilant to both the flows and innovation in the ways in which countries get around sanctions. I can assure the noble Lord, without mentioning specifics, that that will remain at the heart of how we approach this.

title: Household Energy Bills Support
contributions: Tristan Osborne (Chatham and Aylesford) (Lab)
2. What steps she is taking to support households by helping reduce energy bills.
Jim Dickson (Dartford) (Lab)
7. What steps she is taking to support households by helping reduce energy bills.
The Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero (Miatta Fahnbulleh)

We know that people are worried about rising energy bills when the cost of living is biting, and we know that we need to provide breathing space. That is why one of the first things that the Prime Minister did in the job was to scrap VAT on electricity bills. That is on top of the £150 that we took off the cost of energy. We are clear that the scale of what we are seeing requires us to make a concerted effort to get bills down. That is why we are running up clean energy to reduce our exposure to global fossil fuel markets and rolling out the warm homes plan so that we can upgrade our homes. Solar, batteries and clean heat can reduce bills by £600 to £800. Critically, we are determined to put the public back in control of an energy system that the Conservatives lost control of, so that it can work in the interest of consumers.
Tristan Osborne

In Snodland, in my constituency, Octopus Energy is working with social housing tenants to reduce energy bills and cut costs this winter. What more can the Government do, working with the private sector, to promote renewable technologies to reduce bills this winter?
Miatta Fahnbulleh

My hon. Friend is right to give the example of Octopus Energy in his constituency. Through the warm homes plan, we are investing record amounts—billions—in upgrading our homes, because we know that is a key route towards reducing bills. Solar batteries and clean heat insulation can save households between £600 and £800, and we are committed to devolving that to bring about a huge acceleration, street by street, area by area, and estate by estate. That is how we can drive down energy bills for good.
Jim Dickson

Clearly a great deal is being done to protect low-income residents from the effect of rising bills, but given that the energy cap is expected to rise considerably at the start of next year, may I ask the Secretary of State what further conversations she has had with the Treasury to find additional ways of protecting those on the lowest incomes from the effect of rising bills?
Miatta Fahnbulleh

My hon. Friend asks an important question. We are acutely aware that low-income families will be hit hardest by rising prices. We are working with others across Government, including our colleagues in the Treasury, on how we can give people some breathing room. But it is important to emphasise that we have already acted. We have removed VAT from domestic electricity bills, and that comes into force straightaway. We are taking £150 off the cost of bills, and we are also delivering the warm home discount. That means £150 for 6 million of our lowest-earning households. We understand the pressure that households are under, and we will act and stand by people to support them.
Sir Gavin Williamson (Stone, Great Wyrley and Penkridge) (Con)

Many people, not just in my constituency but throughout the country, rely on off-grid energy. I recognise that the Government have taken steps to try and help them, but so many of them have been exposed to massive shocks and leaps in the cost of filling their tanks with oil or gas. Will the Government consider doing a little more to help the many people who are incredibly vulnerable to these energy shocks?
Miatta Fahnbulleh

The right hon. Member raises an important point. We know that families in off-grid households are under huge pressure, and we are taking action to support them. We have put aside £50 million to support, for example, families who use heating oil. We are encouraging households to do that because the uptake has been lower than we want, but we are also introducing regulation of heating oil so that we can protect households. We know that there is more we can do, and we are absolutely committed to getting it done.
Mr Joshua Reynolds (Maidenhead) (LD)

Cornwall Insight forecasts that the energy price cap will increase by a further 16% in January. The Secretary of State has spoken about taking VAT off electricity bills, but that amounts to £45 for an average household. In reality, that is like trying to fill a swimming pool with a thimble—it is not going to work. How will she help to protect families who are already struggling, and will she consider an essential energy guarantee so that all the energy that we need can be affordable for every household?
Miatta Fahnbulleh

We are very clear about where the end destination is. We need to get to an energy system that is affordable for everyone, and we absolutely recognise that the present system is not. We are taking short-term action to give people breathing space, but ultimately I come back to the question of why families are under so much pressure. It is, in fact, because we are acutely exposed to global fossil fuel markets that we do not control. When we talk about clean energy, it is because that is the route by which we get bills down. We have to take the long-term action. We also have to ensure sure that we are reforming the market so that it works in the interests of consumers. We are providing breathing space and standing by people because we need to, but absolutely taking the hard long-term action so that we can fix this problem for good.
Baggy Shanker (Derby South) (Lab/Co-op)

With approximately 15% of Derby South households estimated to be living in fuel poverty, too many families will be dreading higher energy bills as the nights draw in. What reassurances can the Secretary of State offer my constituents that as much help as possible is on its way?
Miatta Fahnbulleh

We know that families across the country will be very worried this winter. I have been to my hon. Friend’s constituency and to constituencies across the country, and I understand the pressure that people are under. We have taken action on breathing space, we will have the £150 warm home discount, and we are driving forward home upgrades because that is the way in which we can get bills down. We are doing that through local authorities. Let no one be in any doubt, however, that we understand that the status quo is untenable, and we will take the action that is necessary to drive bills down.
Robert Jenrick (Newark) (Reform)

Last week, the Secretary of State signed off a massive solar farm in my constituency called the Steeple. It comes on the back of another massive solar farm called One Earth, which was approved by her predecessor earlier in the summer, and a third application sits on her desk today, for a project called Great North Road. In aggregate, if she signs off the latest one, 10% of the entire landmass of my constituency will be solar farms, and my constituents will see no benefit from this in their own energy bills. I wrote to her earlier in the summer to congratulate her on her new position and ask whether she would like to come to my constituency, meet my local residents and make the case for these giant solar farms to my constituents, if she really believes they are in their best interests.
Mr Speaker
Order. The right hon. Member has been here a long time. Please look at the Chair, rather than the person who is answering the question. These are the rules of the House—they are not my rules.
Miatta Fahnbulleh

I gently point out to the right hon. Member that less than 1% of the land will be taken up by solar farms, even under our most ambitious assumptions, but let us come back to the conversation that we are having. Energy bills are too high, and we are far too exposed to global fossil fuel markets. We therefore need home-grown energy that we control. Solar is a cheap and effective way in which we can do that. The right hon. Member may not have a plan, or indeed care about having a plan, to get energy bills down, but we on this side of the House are very clear about what we need to do. Renewables is our route to driving bills down, and that is what the public expect of us.
Mr Speaker
I call the shadow Minister.
Sir Ashley Fox (Bridgwater) (Con)

Britain already has the highest electricity prices in Europe, which makes all our families worse off. The Prime Minister’s decision to end VAT on household electricity bills—for only six months—is a tiny step in the right direction, but the Government need to do much more. Will the Secretary of State reduce household energy bills by £200 a year by adopting the Conservatives’ cheap power plan? Will she extend that VAT cut, axe the carbon tax and scrap renewables obligation contracts, so that all British households are better off?
Miatta Fahnbulleh

I do not think the hon. Member should have mentioned the cheap power plan, which is based on dodgy figures that the Conservatives cannot add up. Candidly, in the spirit of not point scoring, let us examine their record. They were in power for 14 years. They had the opportunity to decouple us from global fossil fuel markets and to invest in clean energy, but they did none of it. We are in this position because of the inaction and failure of the Conservatives, so they should show a bit of humility. They have no plan. Their cheap power plan is based on dodgy numbers and, candidly, we do have a plan for how to get bills down.

title: Social Security (Marriage)
contributions: Motion for leave to bring in a Bill (Standing Order No. 23)
Mr Richard Holden (Basildon and Billericay) (Con)

I beg to move, That leave be given to bring in a Bill to prohibit the recognition of polygamous marriages, marriages within prohibited degrees, and certain other marriages between close relatives, in the social security system. I have brought the Bill to the House to correct an extraordinary fault in our welfare system—one so bizarre and indefensible that I can scarcely believe that we need legislation to address it. We do not yet know what the Government wish to do in this area, but I hope that if the Bill passes today, they will not oppose it on Friday 13 November. We should begin with a simple question: what is welfare for? Beveridge understood the principles of making a contribution, of responsibility, and of providing security for hard times. You pay into a system and help sustain it, and it is there for you when you need it. Alongside that, help is there for those most in need—those who simply cannot or will never be able to look after themselves. That is the essence of a system that Members on all sides of this House could agree to—a system that is contributory and compassionate. How far have we drifted when our rules make special provision for polygamy or incest to be recognised in the benefit system? Can Government Members—or any other Members—point to where in the Beveridge report it is envisaged that a man’s third or fourth wife be supported? Where was any of that when Beveridge laid the foundations of our modern welfare system? Some Members take a different view on Beveridge. They have never seen a benefit of any kind, for anyone, that they did not want preserved at any cost. They are unable or unwilling to say no. Whenever the moment arrives to top up a budget or dish out another handout, those Members are there. I hope that the Bill will stir a new feeling in those Members, and that the blinkers will fall from their eyes. I hope that when they see a system that gives special treatment to men with multiple wives, and potentially to incestuous marriages, their inner conservativism will break out. We are talking about provisions that recognise overseas polygamous marriages and make allowance for additional spouses—a second or third wife and onwards. We are talking about a man rinsing the taxpayer for social security benefits under unbelievable provisions in law that recognise polygamous marriages, which are illegal in the UK. We chuck around welfare payments to such people with abandon. Taxpayers are entitled to ask what on earth we are doing. The Bill is about polygamy, but it is also about overseas marriages between close relatives. To one of my written parliamentary questions, which I know Ministers appreciate dearly, I received an extraordinary answer. What did a Minister say about overseas marriages between an uncle and his niece, or an aunt and her nephew—marriages that are illegal in the UK—being recognised in our welfare budget? They said it was “unlikely”. Frankly, “unlikely” is not good enough, especially when Ministers cannot give me an answer on how many polygamous or incestuous marriages are being supported by our welfare system. The standards at issue here are hardly novel. Bigamy has been a statutory criminal offence in the UK since 1604, more than four centuries ago. Marriages within prohibited degrees, including incestuous ones between uncle and niece or aunt and nephew, were made automatically void by the Marriage Act 1835, nearly two centuries ago. Our modern legislation explicitly outlaws incestuous sexual activity between uncles and nieces or aunts and nephews. When Parliament has rightly drawn those boundaries, surely it is right that our welfare system should uphold them. I have brought to the House this Bill, backed by the Leader of the Opposition and the shadow Work and Pensions Secretary, my hon. Friend the Member for Faversham and Mid Kent (Helen Whately), to end recognition of polygamous marriages and put it beyond doubt that overseas incestuous marriages cannot and should not be recognised in our welfare system for social security purposes. How did we get here, when such marriages are illegal in our country? How did it come about that we recognise them if they were conducted overseas? The situation developed as a result of common-law rules and decisions made by courts. As in so many other areas, these decisions were probably well meaning, but this situation is completely inimical to a cohesive society and a coherent polity, and anathema to the values of our country. The beautiful thing about our country and Parliament is that we are sovereign; Parliament can legislate to remove uncertainty and revoke common law where it is wrong. Parliament must take responsibility. We decide what our welfare system recognises, and that is the signal that this House should send, clearly and explicitly, through the law of this country. Time and again, I meet constituents in Basildon and Billericay who need support, or those on the other side, who are being squeezed more and more by higher taxes—people who work long hours, but who see their bills rise as they try to support their family. Why are my constituents not more deserving of our attention? Instead, we are bundling cash, first class, to men with multiple wives, and to those who made an uncle-niece marriage overseas. Let us take a sensible step to address the issue in a way that recognises the values behind our benefit system, which is rooted in compassion and the principle of contribution, and in the values of our country. It is not there to pay for cultural practices that are illegal here. Surely it is insane that our welfare rules make special provision for men with many wives. I believe that Parliament should put the matter beyond doubt. I hope that the House supports the Bill, and that the Government do not back away from it, but instead support it on its Second Reading on Friday 13 November. Question put and agreed to. Ordered, That Mr Richard Holden, Mrs Kemi Badenoch, Helen Whateley, Claire Coutinho, Laura Trott, Tom Tugendhat, Katie Lam, Dame Rebecca Harris, Joy Morrissey, Andrew Griffith, Nick Timothy and Neil O’Brien present the Bill. Mr Richard Holden accordingly presented the Bill. Bill read the First time; to be read a Second time on Friday 13 November , and to be printed (Bill 1 63 ).
